paragraphs: Adam Smith taught moral philosophy at Glasgow for over a decade before he wrote the book he is remembered for, and his first major work, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, was about sympathy and ethics rather than markets. He later spent two years touring France as a tutor to a young duke, and it was partly conversations with French economists there that shaped his thinking on trade.

The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, argued that individuals pursuing their own interest in a competitive market tend to produce outcomes that benefit everyone, an idea he illustrated with a pin factory where dividing the work into separate steps let a small team make thousands of pins a day rather than a handful.

Aeschylus was born around 525 BCE near Athens and fought as a hoplite at the Battle of Marathon, an experience his epitaph, by his own reported wish, mentioned before any of his plays. He is credited with adding a second actor to tragic performances, which turned recited narration into dialogue and, with it, into drama capable of conflict onstage.

Of roughly eighty plays he is thought to have written, seven survive complete, including the Oresteia, the only full trilogy to come down from Greek tragedy. Ancient sources report he died in Sicily after a tortoise, dropped by an eagle mistaking his bald head for a rock, struck and killed him, a story too neat to trust but repeated for over two thousand years.

Christie began writing detective fiction on a dare from her sister, who doubted she could construct a puzzle nobody could solve before the reveal. Her first novel, The Mysterious Affair at Styles, introduced Hercule Poirot in 1920 and was rejected by several publishers before Bodley Head accepted it.

In December 1926, after her husband asked for a divorce, Christie disappeared for eleven days, sparking a nationwide search involving thousands of volunteers and, briefly, aerial searches. She was found registered under her husband's mistress's surname at a Yorkshire hotel and never explained the episode publicly for the rest of her life.

Akhenaten was born Amenhotep, a younger son of Amenhotep III who was not raised to expect the throne. Some scholars think his elder brother Thutmose, who died young, was meant to rule instead, which would make Akhenaten's accession around 1353 BCE something closer to an accident of succession than a planned reign.

Once crowned, he closed temples to Egypt's other gods, elevated the sun disc Aten above them, and moved the capital to a new city, Akhetaten, built on empty desert land specifically because it belonged to no other god. The move was reversed within a generation of his death, and his name was chiselled from monuments so thoroughly that later king lists skip straight over him.

Alan Turing was born on 23 June 1912 in Paddington, London, while his parents were between postings in colonial India. His 1936 paper on computable numbers described an imaginary machine reading and writing symbols on a tape, years before anyone built one, and it still defines what a computer is and is not able to calculate.

At Bletchley Park he helped design the bombe, an electromechanical machine that sped through the settings German Enigma operators used each day, cutting a search that would have taken humans years down to hours. Convicted in 1952 for a relationship with a man, then a criminal offence in Britain, he lost his security clearance and died in 1954. He received a royal pardon in 2013.

Albert Camus was born on 7 November 1913 in Mondovi, in French Algeria, to a poor pied-noir family; his father died in the First World War before Camus turned one, and he was raised by his mother and grandmother in a home with no running water. He worked as a journalist in Algiers before moving to occupied France, where he edited the Resistance paper Combat under a false name.

He rejected the label existentialist, preferring to describe the absurd: a universe that offers no inherent meaning, met by a human demand for one. The Stranger and The Plague built that idea into fiction rather than argument. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957 at 44, one of its youngest recipients, and died in a car accident less than three years later.

Einstein was born in Ulm in 1879 and, contrary to the enduring myth, was not a poor student, though he did clash with the rote discipline of German schooling and left one institution before his final exams. Unable to secure an academic post after graduating, he took a job examining patent applications in Bern, work he later credited with sharpening his instinct for spotting the flaw in an idea.

In 1905, still a patent clerk, he published four papers in a single year, on light quanta, Brownian motion, special relativity and mass-energy equivalence, any one of which would have made a career. General relativity followed in 1915, and its confirmation during a 1919 solar eclipse, when starlight was shown bending around the sun as his equations predicted, made him a global celebrity almost overnight.

Schweitzer was born in 1875 in Kaysersberg, then part of Germany and now in France, a region whose shifting borders left him fluent in both languages and cultures for life. He had already earned doctorates in philosophy, theology and music, and built a reputation as an organist and scholar of Bach, before deciding at thirty to retrain in medicine so he could work as a missionary doctor.

In 1913 he founded a hospital at Lambarene in French Equatorial Africa, now Gabon, funding much of it himself through lecture tours and organ recitals in Europe. He used his 1952 Nobel Peace Prize money to expand the hospital, and he continued treating patients there into his eighties, a life he summarised with the phrase reverence for life.

Huxley came from a family thick with scientists, his grandfather was the biologist Thomas Henry Huxley, and he intended to become a doctor himself until an eye illness at sixteen left him partially blind and unable to continue lab work. He turned to writing instead, publishing Brave New World in 1932 after a trip to the United States left him unsettled by its consumer culture and mass entertainment.

The novel imagined control through pleasure and engineered contentment rather than fear, a contrast Huxley later drew explicitly against Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four. In 1954 he tried mescaline under a doctor's supervision and wrote The Doors of Perception about the experience, a book that later gave a rock band its name.

Fleming was born on a farm in Ayrshire, Scotland, in 1881 and was an army doctor during the First World War, watching soldiers die of infected wounds that the antiseptics of the time made worse rather than better. That experience shaped the research he pursued afterward at St Mary's Hospital in London, largely on the body's own defences against bacteria.

In 1928 he returned from a holiday to find a mould had contaminated one of his culture dishes and killed the bacteria growing around it, a mess he almost discarded before noticing what it meant. He published the finding but lacked the means to produce the substance, penicillin, in usable quantities, and it took Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, a decade later, to turn it into a working drug.

Alexander Graham Bell was born on 3 March 1847 in Edinburgh into a family of speech specialists, his father the inventor of a phonetic alphabet and his mother and later his wife both deaf, which shaped his lifelong work on elocution and hearing. He emigrated first to Canada and then to Boston, where he taught at a school for the deaf while experimenting with devices to transmit sound electrically.

On 14 February 1876 Bell's lawyer filed a telephone patent application at the US Patent Office; another inventor, Elisha Gray, filed a competing description of a similar device the same day. Bell's paperwork was logged fifth that day and Gray's thirty-ninth, and the patent, granted on 7 March, went to Bell. Lawsuits over the invention ran for years afterward.

Nobel was born in Stockholm in 1833 and grew up largely in St Petersburg, where his father manufactured explosives and machinery. Nobel invented dynamite in 1867 by stabilising the wildly unpredictable explosive nitroglycerin with an absorbent mineral, making it safe enough to transport and detonate on command, and he patented the process across Europe and the United States.

In 1888 a French newspaper mistakenly reported his own death instead of his brother Ludvig's, running an obituary that called him a man who could hardly be considered a benefactor of humanity. Whether that specific story pushed him toward his final decision is disputed, but his 1895 will did leave most of his fortune to fund prizes in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace.

Earhart's 1932 transatlantic solo flight nearly ended in Northern Ireland fields rather than an airfield: instrument trouble and ice forced her down early, and she landed in a pasture in County Londonderry, startling a farmhand who asked if she had flown far. She had crossed from Newfoundland in under fifteen hours.

In July 1937 she disappeared over the central Pacific attempting to circle the globe with navigator Fred Noonan, last heard reporting low fuel near Howland Island. The US Navy's search, one of the largest and most expensive of its era, found no trace of the plane, and no confirmed wreckage has been recovered since.

Amerigo Vespucci was born in Florence in 1454 and worked as a Medici business agent in Seville before joining Spanish and Portuguese expeditions to the coast of South America around 1499 to 1502. Unlike Columbus, he argued in his own published letters that the land was a previously unknown continent, not the edge of Asia.

Those letters reached the German cartographer Martin Waldseemuller, whose 1507 world map labelled the new continent America, a Latinised form of Amerigo, in credit to that claim. Vespucci never knew the name had been given: he died in 1512, and the mapmaker himself later tried to withdraw the label once Columbus's earlier voyage became better known, by which point it had already spread too far to recall.

Hans Christian Andersen was born in Odense, Denmark, on 2 April 1805, the son of a poor shoemaker, and left home at fourteen with almost nothing to try his luck as an actor and singer in Copenhagen. A wealthy patron eventually noticed him and paid for the schooling his family never could, though Andersen struggled with it as an older, awkward pupil among much younger classmates.

He wrote novels and plays first and considered them his serious work, but the fairy tales, published in small instalments from 1835 onward, outlasted everything else he wrote. Tales of a mermaid who trades her voice for legs and a duckling mocked until it grows into a swan drew on Danish folk tradition but were largely his own invention, echoing his own outsider childhood. He never married, and left a fortune to his family when he died in 1875.

Carnegie was born in Dunfermline, Scotland, in 1835 into a family of weavers who emigrated to Pennsylvania when he was twelve after machine looms wiped out their trade. He worked his way up from a bobbin boy in a cotton mill to building the Carnegie Steel Company into the dominant American steel producer, which he sold to J.P. Morgan in 1901 for roughly 480 million dollars.

His essay The Gospel of Wealth argued that the rich were obligated to give their fortunes away during their lifetime rather than leave them to heirs. He spent his last two decades doing exactly that, funding more than 2,500 public libraries across the English-speaking world along with concert halls, universities and a peace endowment. He died in 1919, having given away most of his fortune.

Andrew Jackson was born in the Carolina backcountry in 1767, orphaned by his early teens, and captured as a boy courier during the Revolutionary War, an experience that left him with a British officer's sabre scar and a lasting hatred of the crown.

He built his national fame as a general, most of all at New Orleans in January 1815, a battle fought after the peace treaty had already been signed but before word of it reached the armies. As president from 1829 he expanded the vote for white men, fought the national bank, and forced the Cherokee and other nations west on the Trail of Tears.

Andy Warhol was born Andrew Warhola on 6 August 1928 in Pittsburgh to working-class Slovak immigrant parents, and began his career as a commercial illustrator drawing shoe advertisements in New York. He turned that background in mass production into subject matter, choosing a Campbell's soup can, a grocery item he said he ate for lunch nearly every day, as fine art.

His studio, the Factory, employed assistants to silkscreen his images in multiples, deliberately blurring the line between an original and a copy that painting had always assumed. He photographed and filmed the celebrities, drag performers and hangers-on who passed through it, and survived being shot there in 1968 by a writer with a grievance against him, an attack that left him in lasting pain.

Anne Frank was born on 12 June 1929 in Frankfurt, Germany, to a Jewish family that fled to Amsterdam after the Nazis took power, arriving there in stages by early 1934. In July 1942 her family went into hiding in a concealed annexe above her father's office, joined later by four other Jews, and stayed there for just over two years before being betrayed to the Gestapo.

The diary she kept during that time, written first for herself and then revised with an eye to eventual publication, survived because a family friend gathered her papers from the ransacked annexe after the arrest. Anne died at Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in early 1945, weeks before its liberation. Her father Otto, the only member of the household to survive, had the diary published in 1947.

Anton Chekhov was born on 29 January 1860 in Taganrog, a port town on the Sea of Azov, the son of a grocer whose failing shop left the family in debt. Chekhov trained and practised as a doctor, writing comic sketches for magazines under pen names to support his medical studies, and he treated patients even after tuberculosis had begun to weaken him.

His early plays were poorly received; the 1896 premiere of The Seagull was jeered so badly that Chekhov left the theatre before it ended. Its later staging by the Moscow Art Theatre, directed by Konstantin Stanislavski, rescued the play and set the template for The Cherry Orchard and Three Sisters, works built on ordinary conversation rather than dramatic incident.

Antonio Vivaldi was ordained a priest in 1703 but stopped saying Mass within a year, citing chest trouble that may have been asthma, and spent most of his career instead running the orchestra at a Venetian orphanage for girls, the Ospedale della Pieta. The institution's concerts became one of the city's biggest musical draws, with the girls performing hidden behind a grille.

The Four Seasons, published in 1725 as part of a larger set, came with sonnets describing storms, hunts and barking dogs that the music was written to match, an unusually literal kind of programme music for its time. Vivaldi died in Vienna in 1741, largely forgotten by then, and was buried in a pauper's grave; his manuscripts were rediscovered only in the twentieth century.

Archimedes was born around 287 BCE in Syracuse, on Sicily, and studied for a time in Alexandria before returning home to work under the patronage of the city's king. Most of what is known about his life comes from later biographers, especially Plutarch, writing well over a century after his death.

He calculated a close approximation of pi, worked out the mathematics behind levers and buoyancy, and designed war machines that, according to Roman accounts, helped Syracuse hold off a siege for two years. He was killed in 212 BCE when the city finally fell, reportedly by a Roman soldier he had ignored while absorbed in a geometry problem drawn in sand.

Aristophanes was born around 446 BCE and began staging comedies in Athens while barely out of his teens, a fact he later joked about in prologues addressed directly to the audience. Eleven of his roughly forty plays survive, the only complete examples of Old Comedy to come down from antiquity at all.

Lysistrata, in which Athenian and Spartan women withhold sex to force an end to war, was staged in 411 BCE, during a real and increasingly desperate phase of the Peloponnesian War. His comedies mocked living politicians and philosophers by name onstage, including Socrates in The Clouds, a satire performed while its target was still walking the streets of Athens.

Aristotle was born in 384 BCE in Stagira, in northern Greece, the son of a physician at the Macedonian court, a connection that later put him in position to tutor the young Alexander the Great around 343 BCE. He studied at Plato's Academy for two decades before leaving, reportedly passed over for its leadership after Plato's death.

His surviving works, many likely lecture notes rather than polished treatises, cover logic, biology, ethics, politics and physics, and shaped European university curricula so thoroughly that medieval scholars simply called him the Philosopher, no name required. Much of his biology, based on direct dissection, held up better under later scrutiny than his physics did.

Arthur Conan Doyle was born in Edinburgh on 22 May 1859 and trained as a physician before he ever published fiction, and one of his medical teachers, Joseph Bell, gave him a model for a detective who diagnosed strangers from small physical details. Doyle's practice was slow enough that he wrote his first Holmes novel, A Study in Scarlet, while waiting for patients.

He grew to resent his own creation, killing Holmes off at the Reichenbach Falls in 1893 to write historical fiction instead, only to bring him back eight years later under public pressure. Doyle also spent much of his later life defending spiritualism and fairies, campaigns that cost him credibility but never dented the character he had come to regard as a distraction from his real ambitions.

Ashoka was born around 304 BCE into the Mauryan royal family and came to the throne after a succession struggle that, by some later Buddhist accounts, involved killing rival brothers, though the details vary between sources written centuries afterward. His early reign as emperor continued the aggressive expansion his grandfather Chandragupta had begun.

That changed with the conquest of Kalinga around 261 BCE, a war so costly that Ashoka's own rock edicts, inscriptions he had carved across the subcontinent, describe his remorse and his subsequent turn to Buddhist principles of non-violence. Those edicts, written in vernacular languages rather than the usual courtly Sanskrit, are also some of the earliest surviving Indian texts addressed directly to ordinary subjects.

Attila was born around 406 CE somewhere in the Hunnic territories north of the Danube; no Roman or Hunnic source records the place, and most of what is known about his early life comes from Roman diplomats who dealt with him as an adult rather than any account of his childhood. He ruled jointly with his brother Bleda from 434 CE until having him killed around 445 CE.

Roman writers who met him in person, notably the envoy Priscus, described a court of considerable wealth surrounding a leader who dressed plainly and ate from wooden plates while his officers used gold and silver. Attila's raids reached deep into both the Eastern and Western empires before he died in 453 CE, reportedly of a nosebleed on his wedding night, and his empire fragmented among his sons within a year.

Audrey Hepburn was born Audrey Kathleen Ruston in Brussels in 1929, the daughter of a Dutch baroness and an English banker with fascist sympathies who abandoned the family when she was six. She spent part of her childhood in Nazi-occupied Arnhem, where food was scarce enough in the final winter of the war that she later said she ate tulip bulbs and suffered lasting anaemia and breathing problems from malnutrition.

That wartime hunger shaped her later work as a UNICEF goodwill ambassador, which she took up in 1988 after her acting career had largely wound down, travelling to Ethiopia, Sudan and Somalia during famine and civil conflict. She trained as a ballet dancer before turning to acting, and her Broadway role in Gigi, not a film, was what first brought her to Hollywood's attention.

Auguste Rodin was born on 12 November 1840 in Paris to a working-class family, and he failed the entrance exam to the city's leading art school three times. He spent years as an ornament carver for other sculptors before his own work found an audience, well into his thirties by the time he had any independent reputation at all.

The Thinker began as a single figure atop a much larger, unfinished commission called The Gates of Hell, meant to show Dante looking down over the damned. Rodin left many of his surfaces rough and unpolished, a deliberate break from the smooth, idealised nudes that dominated official French sculpture, and it is that unfinished, working texture that later sculptors pointed to as the start of a modern approach.

Honore de Balzac was born in Tours on 20 May 1799 and added the aristocratic de himself later in life; his family had no noble blood behind it. He trained as a law clerk, tried and failed at several businesses, including a printing venture that left him deep in debt, and turned to writing largely because it was the way out.

He conceived The Human Comedy as a single connected project spanning close to a hundred novels and stories, with characters reappearing across volumes to build a continuous portrait of French society after Napoleon's fall. He wrote at night on enormous quantities of coffee, sometimes fifty cups a day, a schedule that wore his health down early. He died in 1850, five months after marrying a woman he had courted by letter for nearly two decades.

Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770 into a musical but troubled household; his father, also a court musician, drilled him hard and drank away much of the family's money. He moved to Vienna in his early twenties to study, briefly, with Haydn.

His hearing began failing in his late twenties and was largely gone within two decades, yet he kept composing by feeling vibrations through the piano and by memory of sound, producing the Ninth Symphony after he could no longer hear an orchestra play it. He never married, and his personal life was marked by a long, bitter custody fight over his nephew Karl.

Benjamin Franklin left school at ten and was mostly self-taught, apprenticed to his brother's Boston print shop before running away to Philadelphia at seventeen with almost no money. He built a printing and publishing business there, made himself wealthy enough by his early forties to retire from trade, and spent the rest of his life on science, diplomacy and public projects.

His 1752 kite experiment, drawing a spark from a thundercloud to prove lightning was electrical, is often exaggerated; he never claimed to have been struck, and the version usually told compresses a longer set of experiments he ran with a kite, a key and a Leyden jar. He later was the American envoy to France during the Revolutionary War, using his fame there to help secure the alliance that helped win it.

Russell was born in 1872 into an aristocratic family that had produced prime ministers, and he outlived both his parents by the time he was four, raised afterward by his grandmother. He spent years with Alfred North Whitehead trying to derive the whole of mathematics from a small set of logical axioms, producing the three volumes of Principia Mathematica, which reportedly sold so few copies that the pair lost money on it.

He was jailed briefly in 1918 for an article opposing the war, and again decades later, at nearly ninety, for a protest against nuclear weapons. He wrote on subjects far outside logic, from marriage to happiness, and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950 for that broader body of work rather than for the technical philosophy he considered his real achievement.

Betty Friedan was born Bettye Goldstein on 4 February 1921 in Peoria, Illinois, and worked as a labour journalist before marriage and motherhood pushed her out of that career. Preparing for her Smith College reunion in 1957, she surveyed her former classmates and found many of them, like her, privately unhappy despite living the suburban life magazines told them to want.

The Feminine Mystique, published in 1963, named that unhappiness what she called the problem that has no name and argued it came from women being denied identity outside the home. The book sold in the millions and helped launch what became known as second-wave feminism. Friedan co-founded the National Organization for Women in 1966 and was its first president.

Bob Marley was born in 1945 in Nine Mile, a rural district in Jamaica's Saint Ann Parish, the son of a Black Jamaican mother and a white Jamaican father in his sixties whom he barely knew growing up. He moved with his mother to Trench Town, a poor Kingston neighbourhood, as a boy, and it was there that he met Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer, with whom he formed the Wailers in 1963.

Marley's Rastafari faith, which he adopted in the mid-1960s, shaped both his lyrics and his image, including the dreadlocks and reasoning sessions that became inseparable from his public persona. He survived an assassination attempt at his Kingston home in 1976, two days before a concert intended to ease political violence, and performed at the show anyway with a bullet fragment still in his arm.

Giovanni Boccaccio was born in 1313, likely in Florence or nearby Certaldo, the illegitimate son of a merchant who sent him to Naples to train in banking and law. Neither trade held his attention; he spent his time at the Angevin court instead, reading and writing romances among a circle of aristocrats and scholars.

The Decameron, written in the years after the Black Death reached Florence in 1348, frames its hundred stories as tales told by ten young people who have fled the plague-stricken city for a country villa. Boccaccio had watched the epidemic firsthand, and his introduction describing bodies left in the streets is one of the most cited eyewitness accounts of the outbreak.

Booker T. Washington was born into slavery on 5 April 1856 on a Virginia plantation and did not learn his exact birth date; he chose the year himself later from family memory. Freed as a child after the Civil War, he worked in salt furnaces and coal mines while teaching himself to read, then walked much of the roughly 500 miles to the Hampton Institute to get an education.

In 1881 he was chosen to lead a new Black teacher-training school in Alabama, which opened in a shanty and a hen house with thirty students. Tuskegee grew under his direction into a major institution, built partly by student labour. Washington argued that economic self-sufficiency should come before agitation for civil rights, a stance that made him the era's most powerful Black leader in white eyes and drew sharp criticism from W.E.B. Du Bois.

No record gives the exact day. The surviving document is a baptism entry from a Milan parish in late September 1571, and historians lean on his given name, Michelangelo, the feast day of the archangel falling on the 29th, to guess at a birthday nobody wrote down. For centuries painters had assumed he came from the town of Caravaggio; the baptism record, found only in the twentieth century, put him in Milan instead.

He took the town's name as his own once he left it, and the confusion says something about how thin the paper trail is for a man whose paintings are so vivid. Court records survive in far greater number than personal ones: brawls, a sword charge, eventually a killing in Rome in 1606. The light and shadow that made his altarpieces famous have no equivalent biography behind them, just scattered civic ink.

Jung was born in Switzerland in 1875, the son of a pastor, and trained as a psychiatrist at a hospital in Zurich where he studied word association tests to probe unconscious thought. He became a close collaborator of Sigmund Freud, initially seen as his likely successor, until the two split acrimoniously around 1913 over Jung's doubts that sexuality explained everything Freud claimed it did.

Working largely alone afterward, he developed his own framework built around archetypes, personality types later popularised as introversion and extraversion, and a collective unconscious he argued was shared across all humanity rather than built from one person's own experience. His ideas spread well beyond clinical psychology, into literature, religious studies and, eventually, the Myers-Briggs personality test.

Carl Sagan was born in Brooklyn in 1934 and traced his fascination with space to a visit to the 1939 World's Fair and to reading science fiction by writers like Edgar Rice Burroughs. He worked on NASA's Mariner, Viking and Voyager missions, helped design the plaques and records those spacecraft carried, and pushed for the Viking landers to search Martian soil for signs of life.

His television series Cosmos, broadcast in 1980, was watched by hundreds of millions of people worldwide and made him the most recognisable scientist of his era. He co-founded the Planetary Society in 1980 and spent decades arguing that searching for extraterrestrial radio signals, SETI, deserved serious funding rather than dismissal as fringe.

Charles Babbage was born in London on 26 December 1791, the son of a banker, and grew up obsessively bothered by errors in printed mathematical tables, the kind of small copying mistake that could send a ship off course. That irritation became a career: he set out to build a machine that calculated by turning a crank rather than a clerk's pen.

The Difference Engine got funding from the British government and never got finished; the far more ambitious Analytical Engine, designed to be programmed with punched cards, existed only on paper. Ada Lovelace wrote notes on it describing what a general-purpose computer might do beyond arithmetic. The London Science Museum finally built a working Difference Engine from his drawings in 1991, more than a century after his death, and it ran.

De Gaulle was a little-known brigadier general when France fell in June 1940. He flew to London and broadcast an appeal on the BBC on 18 June urging the French to keep fighting, a speech almost no one in France heard live but which later became the founding myth of the Resistance.

He resigned as president in 1946 rather than accept a constitution he thought left the executive too weak, then returned to power in 1958 amid a crisis over Algeria and wrote a new one, the Fifth Republic's, that gave the president far greater authority. He held that office until resigning in 1969 after losing a referendum on regional reform.

Charles Dickens was born in Portsmouth on 7 February 1812, and when he was twelve his father was imprisoned for debt, forcing the family into poverty and sending Charles to work pasting labels onto bottles of shoe polish in a factory. He kept the experience secret for most of his adult life, ashamed of it even after he had become the most famous novelist in England.

He published most of his novels in monthly or weekly instalments, writing under deadline while readers on both sides of the Atlantic waited for the next chapter. Oliver Twist and A Christmas Carol drew directly on the poverty, workhouses, and child labour he had seen firsthand, and his public readings from his own work drew huge crowds and are thought to have hastened the stroke that killed him in 1870.

Lindbergh flew from New York to Paris in May 1927 in a single-seat monoplane with no forward window, navigating by dead reckoning and a periscope because a fuel tank blocked his direct view ahead. The flight took just under thirty-four hours, much of it in fog and near ice, and he later admitted to hallucinating from exhaustion over the Atlantic.

The fame that followed turned tragic five years later, when his infant son was kidnapped from the family's New Jersey home and later found dead, a case that led to some of the most sweeping press coverage of the era and a new federal kidnapping law. Lindbergh's later isolationist speeches and prewar visits to Germany, including acceptance of a medal from Hermann Goring, cost him much of the public goodwill his flight had earned.

Chaplin was born into poverty in south London; his mother was committed to an asylum and he spent time in a workhouse as a boy before joining a music hall troupe that toured to America. He created the Tramp's costume, the bowler, cane, and too-tight coat, in 1914 by borrowing pieces from other actors at the Keystone studio minutes before a scene.

He never fully embraced sound film, releasing City Lights in 1931 and Modern Times in 1936 as essentially silent works years after the industry had moved on. In 1952, travelling to Britain, he learned his US re-entry permit had been revoked amid suspicion over his politics, and he did not return to America for twenty years.

Geoffrey Chaucer was born around 1343 in London, the son of a wine merchant, not a poet's usual background. He entered royal service as a young man, was captured and ransomed during a campaign in France, and spent much of his working life as a customs official and diplomat rather than a full-time writer.

The Canterbury Tales, unfinished at his death in 1400, was written in Middle English at a time when French and Latin still dominated serious literature in England. Framing it as stories told by pilgrims of every social rank, from knight to miller to nun, let him mimic a range of voices in one book, which is part of why it is still read as much for its variety as for any single tale.

Claude Monet was born on 14 November 1840 in Paris and grew up in the Normandy port of Le Havre, where his father wanted him to go into the family grocery trade. He drew constantly instead, and a local painter, Eugene Boudin, talked him into working outdoors directly from the landscape rather than composing from sketches in a studio, a habit Monet kept for the rest of his life.

In 1874 a group of painters the official Salon had rejected staged their own show in Paris, and a critic mocked one of Monet's harbour scenes, titled simply Impression, Sunrise, as unfinished mush. The label stuck to the whole group as an insult and was worn as a name instead. Monet kept painting the same subjects, haystacks, water lilies, Rouen Cathedral, at different hours to track how light alone changed what was in front of him.

Christopher Columbus was born in Genoa in 1451, the son of a wool weaver, and went to sea as a teenager on merchant voyages around the Mediterranean and later the Atlantic coast. He spent years pitching a westward route to Asia to the Portuguese and Spanish crowns before Isabella and Ferdinand finally financed him in 1492, after their own experts had rejected his distance calculations as badly wrong.

He never reached Asia and never accepted that the land he found was not part of it. Later voyages turned into disputes over his governorship of Hispaniola, brutal enough toward the Indigenous population that he was arrested and sent back to Spain in chains in 1500, though restored to some privileges before his death in 1506.

Constantine was born in 272 CE in Naissus, in the Balkans, to Constantius, a Roman military officer who would later become emperor, and Helena, a woman of low social status whom Constantius set aside for a more advantageous marriage. Constantine was proclaimed emperor by his father's troops in 306 CE and then spent nearly two decades fighting rivals to make that claim real across the whole empire.

In 313 CE he issued the Edict of Milan with his co-emperor Licinius, ending state persecution of Christians and returning confiscated property to the church, though he did not make Christianity the empire's official religion himself. In 330 CE he dedicated a new capital on the site of the old Greek city of Byzantium, renaming it Constantinople after himself.

Nicolaus Copernicus was born in 1473 in Torun, in the Kingdom of Poland, and trained not as an astronomer by profession but as a church administrator, studying canon law and medicine alongside mathematics at universities in Krakow and Italy. Astronomy was closer to a private obsession he pursued around his official duties as a cathedral canon in Frombork.

He worked out his heliocentric model decades before publishing it, circulating an early sketch privately and only agreeing to print the full argument, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, in 1543, the year he died. Legend holds he saw a finished copy on his deathbed. The book unsettled almost no one immediately; the real disruption came later, once Galileo and Kepler built on it.

Cosimo de' Medici was born in Florence in 1389 into a banking family that was wealthy but not yet politically dominant. His father Giovanni had built the bank into the pope's financier of choice; Cosimo inherited that business and, briefly exiled by rival families in 1433, returned within a year to control the city without ever holding formal office himself.

He ran Florence through allies placed in elected posts and through the bank's leverage over anyone who owed the Medici money, a model his descendants would refine for generations. His patronage funded Brunelleschi's architecture and the Medici library's manuscript hunting, and he personally backed the Platonic Academy that helped revive Greek philosophy in the city.

Cyrus was born around 600 BCE, the son of a Persian vassal king under the Median empire; the famous legend that his grandfather Astyages ordered him killed as an infant, only for a herdsman to raise him instead, comes from Herodotus writing over a century later and reads more like a folk tale pattern than history.

What is documented independently is his conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE and the Cyrus Cylinder, a clay foundation text in which he presents himself as a liberator of the city's gods and people rather than a destroyer. It has since been read, sometimes overread, as an early statement on religious tolerance, though it was also standard Mesopotamian propaganda for a new king.

The 14th Dalai Lama was born Lhamo Thondup to a farming family in Taktser, in the Amdo region of Tibet, in 1935. A search party sent to find the reincarnation of the previous Dalai Lama, who had died two years earlier, tested him at around age two by presenting him with pairs of objects, including the previous Dalai Lama's rosary and a decoy, and he reportedly identified the correct ones without hesitation.

He was enthroned as Tibet's spiritual and temporal leader at fifteen, just as Chinese forces entered Tibet in 1950, and fled to India in 1959 after a failed uprising, where he has lived in exile in Dharamshala ever since. The Nobel committee awarded him the Peace Prize in 1989 for his consistent opposition to violence in seeking Tibetan autonomy.

Dante was born in Florence in 1265 into a minor noble family already reduced in fortune. He trained as a poet and became active in the city's factional politics, holding elected office before backing the losing side in a dispute between rival Guelph factions. In 1302 he was condemned to exile on invented corruption charges and never set foot in Florence again.

The Divine Comedy was written entirely during that exile, moving between the courts of patrons in Verona and Ravenna. Writing it in Tuscan Italian rather than Latin was itself a choice that helped fix the dialect as the basis of the modern Italian language, long before any political unification made that outcome obvious.

Darius was born around 550 BCE to a noble Achaemenid family, not the direct royal line, and took the Persian throne in 522 BCE by killing a man he claimed was an imposter occupying it. The Behistun Inscription, a monumental relief he had carved into a cliff face, tells this version of events in three languages, in Darius's own words, which makes it useful history and unreliable evidence at once.

Once in power he reorganised the empire into provinces called satrapies, standardised coinage and taxation, and began building Persepolis as a ceremonial capital. The palace complex, excavated from the nineteenth century onward, still shows the reliefs of tribute-bearers from across the empire that Darius commissioned to advertise its reach.

David Bowie was born David Robert Jones in Brixton, London, in 1947, and took his stage name in 1966 to avoid confusion with Davy Jones of the Monkees. A schoolyard fight over a girl left him with a permanently dilated left pupil after a punch damaged the muscles around his eye, giving his eyes their famously mismatched appearance rather than any difference in colour, as is often assumed.

He spent years as a minor figure on the London music scene before Space Oddity became a hit in 1969, timed to coincide with the Apollo 11 moon landing. Ziggy Stardust, the alien rock star persona he adopted in 1972, was retired abruptly at a 1973 concert when he announced onstage, to his own band's surprise, that it was the last show they would ever play as that act.

David Hume's A Treatise of Human Nature, published when he was in his late twenties, argued that causation itself is not something we observe but a habit of mind: we see one event follow another repeatedly and assume a necessary connection that the senses never actually show us. The book sold poorly and Hume later said it fell dead-born from the press.

He had far more success as a historian, and his multi-volume History of England was the bestselling account of the country's past for decades after his death in 1776. His scepticism about miracles and religious belief made him too controversial for a university post in his lifetime, and he was passed over for chairs at both Edinburgh and Glasgow largely on those grounds.

Rene Descartes spent most of his working life in the Dutch Republic rather than France, moving house repeatedly because he disliked visitors and wanted quiet to think. He is credited with fusing algebra and geometry into what became analytic geometry, letting curves and shapes be described as equations, a shift that later let Newton and Leibniz build calculus on top of it.

His famous claim that thought is the one thing a mind cannot doubt away, cogito ergo sum, came from a method of stripping every belief down to see what survived scepticism. He died in Stockholm in February 1650, having gone there to tutor Queen Christina, reportedly worn down by the queen's insistence on lessons at five in the morning through a Swedish winter he was not built for.

Lawrence was born in Eastwood, a Nottinghamshire coal town, the son of a miner and a former schoolteacher who pushed him toward books rather than the pit. That gap between his parents shaped his fiction: Sons and Lovers, published in 1913, drew directly on his own upbringing and his mother's grip on him.

Lady Chatterley's Lover, printed privately in Italy in 1928, could not be sold openly in Britain until 1960, when Penguin's unabridged edition was prosecuted under the Obscene Publications Act. The jury acquitted the publisher after eleven days, and the trial is often treated as the moment British censorship of literature effectively ended.

Rivera trained in Europe and painted like a Cubist for over a decade before returning to Mexico in 1921 and abandoning the style almost overnight. The government of the new revolutionary state was commissioning murals for public buildings, and Rivera, unlike most of his peers, wanted an audience that could not afford a gallery ticket.

His 1933 mural for the Rockefeller Center in New York included a portrait of Lenin. The Rockefellers ordered it removed when Rivera refused to take the face out, and workers destroyed the finished mural with axes months after it was covered over. Rivera repainted a version of it in Mexico City the following year.

Diogenes was born around 412 BCE in Sinope, on the Black Sea coast, and arrived in Athens, by most accounts, after being exiled from his home city over a coin-debasing scandal involving his father's mint. Poverty in Athens became the philosophy itself rather than an accident of it.

Ancient biographers say he lived in a large ceramic storage jar rather than a house, walked the streets in daylight carrying a lamp claiming to search for an honest man, and once, told by Plato that a plucked chicken fit Plato's own definition of a featherless biped, brought one into the Academy's lecture hall. Most of this comes from Diogenes Laertius, writing centuries later, and the stories were likely already sharpened into legend by then.

Shostakovich kept a packed suitcase by his door for years after Pravda denounced his opera Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District in 1936 as chaotic and formalist, an attack that could easily have preceded an arrest during the purges. Colleagues and friends of his were disappearing; he later said he expected to be taken away by the secret police at night.

His Fifth Symphony, premiered in 1937, was billed as a Soviet artist's creative response to just criticism and restored his standing, though listeners still argue over whether its triumphant finale is sincere or bitterly ironic. He kept writing symphonies and string quartets that carried private grief and coded protest under officially acceptable surfaces for the rest of his career under Stalin and his successors.

Antonin Dvorak was born on 8 September 1841 in Nelahozeves, a village north of Prague where his father ran the local inn and butcher shop and expected his son to take over the trade. Dvorak trained as a butcher himself before his talent on violin and organ won him a place at Prague's organ school, and he spent years playing viola in theatre orchestras before composing brought in enough to live on.

He spent 1892 to 1895 directing a conservatory in New York, where he wrote the Symphony No. 9, subtitled From the New World, drawing on spirituals and what he understood of Native American melody rather than quoting them. He returned to Bohemia in 1895 and kept folk idiom at the centre of his work for the rest of his career, treating it as material on equal footing with the German symphonic tradition he had trained in.

Eisenhower had never commanded troops in combat before the Second World War; his career before 1941 was staff work and planning, which is exactly what made him the officer Roosevelt and Marshall trusted to hold together an alliance of touchy generals. As Supreme Commander he set the D-Day invasion date around weather reports and postponed it once, on 4 June 1944, before ordering the crossing for the 6th.

As president from 1953, he warned in his own farewell address in 1961 about the growing power of what he named the military-industrial complex, a phrase coined by a former general who had spent the preceding decade building up American defence spending himself.

Edgar Poe was born in Boston on 19 January 1809 to travelling actors, and was orphaned before he turned three; he was taken in, but never legally adopted, by a Richmond merchant named John Allan, whose surname he added to his own. The two quarrelled for years over money, and Allan cut him off after he ran up gambling debts at university and later left West Point.

Poe scraped by as a magazine editor and critic, work that paid poorly and rarely on time, while writing the stories that made his name posthumously. His 1841 story The Murders in the Rue Morgue is generally credited as the first modern detective story, built around a reasoning investigator decades before Holmes. He died in Baltimore in 1849 under circumstances still argued over, found delirious in someone else's clothes days before he died.

Degas was born in Paris in 1834 to a banking family and trained in the strict academic tradition before drifting toward the Impressionists, though he disliked the label and preferred to call himself a realist. He exhibited with the group for years while insisting his real subject was line and movement, not the outdoor light they were known for.

He gained access to the Paris Opera's rehearsal rooms and returned to ballet dancers obsessively, producing more than 1,500 works on the subject across pastels, paintings and small wax sculptures never meant for public display. Failing eyesight pushed him toward sculpture in his later decades, and he died in Paris in 1917, largely blind and reclusive.

Edmund Burke was born in Dublin in 1729 to a Protestant father and a Catholic mother, a mixed household that later shaped his lifelong arguments for tolerance. He trained as a lawyer before turning to writing and politics, entering the House of Commons in 1765 as a Whig.

He is remembered less for any single act than for a body of argument: he defended the American colonists' grievances before 1776, prosecuted the East India Company's abuses in Bengal, and then, in 1790, denounced the French Revolution's abstract rights in Reflections on the Revolution in France. That last book made him, after his death, a founding reference for conservative thought.

Edvard Munch was born on 12 December 1863 in the Norwegian village of Adalsbruk, into a family shadowed by illness: his mother and a sister both died of tuberculosis before he was fourteen, and Munch later wrote that sickness and death stood by his cradle. He trained in Oslo and travelled to Paris, where exposure to Impressionism pushed him toward a rawer, more personal style.

He described the moment behind The Scream as a walk at sunset when he felt nature convulse into a scream, and he painted several versions of the image between 1893 and 1910. One pastel version, sold at auction in 2012, brought nearly 120 million dollars, and two painted versions have separately been stolen from Norwegian museums and later recovered.

Eli Whitney was born in Massachusetts in 1765 and built his cotton gin in 1793 while visiting a Georgia plantation, mechanising the slow hand separation of cotton fibre from seed. He patented it in March 1794, but rampant copying meant it earned him little money.

The gin made short-staple cotton profitable across the South, and demand for the labour to grow and pick it expanded American slavery rather than reducing it. Whitney later took a government contract to build muskets and pushed manufacturing toward interchangeable parts, though the ten-year job took five times longer than he had promised.

Elizabeth Taylor was born in London in 1932 to American parents and moved to Los Angeles with her family in 1939 as war approached in Europe. MGM signed her at nine, and she became one of the studio's biggest child stars in National Velvet, filmed when she was twelve after production delays let her grow tall enough to ride convincingly.

Her activism began close to home: after her friend Rock Hudson died of AIDS in 1985, she co-founded the American Foundation for AIDS Research and later her own foundation, at a time when few public figures would say the disease's name. She testified before Congress for AIDS funding and helped raise hundreds of millions of dollars for research and care, work she continued for the rest of her life alongside her later, less frequent film roles.

Elvis Presley was born in a two-room shack in East Tupelo, Mississippi, in 1935. He had a twin brother, Jesse Garon, who was stillborn about half an hour before him and was buried in an unmarked grave the family could not afford to mark properly, a loss his mother Gladys spoke of for the rest of her life.

The family was poor even by the standards of Depression-era Mississippi; his father served time for altering a cheque when Elvis was a child, and they later moved to Memphis partly to escape the stigma. Presley first recorded at Sun Studio in 1953 not as an audition but paying to cut a two-sided acetate as a birthday present, a session that led producer Sam Phillips to remember his voice when he needed a singer the following year.

Emily Bronte published under a man's name, Ellis Bell, because she and her sisters believed reviewers judged women's writing differently. Wuthering Heights appeared in 1847 to reviews that called it coarse and disagreeable. It sold poorly in her lifetime and only found its reputation after her death.

She was born in Thornton, Yorkshire, in 1818, and grew up on the edge of the moors at Haworth, where her father was the parish curate. She died of tuberculosis in December 1848, aged 30, having reportedly refused a doctor until the day before her death. Wuthering Heights was her only novel.

Dickinson was born in Amherst, Massachusetts, in 1830 and published fewer than a dozen poems in her lifetime, most anonymously and against her wishes. She spent her later decades almost entirely inside her family's house, communicating with visitors sometimes through a door left ajar rather than a face-to-face meeting.

After her death in 1886, her sister Lavinia found nearly 1,800 poems folded into small hand-sewn booklets in a bureau drawer. Dickinson's editors initially smoothed her unconventional dashes and slant rhymes into conventional verse for publication; only in the 20th century did scholars restore her original, stranger punctuation, which is now considered central to how her poems work.

Fermi taught himself calculus from a used book he found at a Rome market stall at fourteen, after his brother's sudden death left him retreating into mathematics. He entered university at seventeen already knowing more physics than some of his examiners, and his doctoral thesis at the Scuola Normale Superiore in Pisa was reportedly the strongest the school had received in years.

In December 1942, under the stands of an abandoned squash court at the University of Chicago, Fermi's team achieved the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction inside Chicago Pile-1, built from graphite blocks and uranium slugs stacked by hand. He had left Italy in 1938, ostensibly to collect his Nobel Prize in Stockholm, and simply did not return, since his wife Laura was Jewish and Mussolini's race laws had just taken effect.

Epicurus was born on the island of Samos in 341 BCE to Athenian parents settled there as colonists, and he studied philosophy under teachers linked to Democritus's atomist tradition before founding his own school in Athens around 306 BCE. He called it the Garden, and unusually for the time it admitted women and enslaved people as members alongside free men.

His idea of pleasure as life's aim is often misremembered as indulgence, but his own writings recommend simple food, steady friendships and freedom from fear of death and the gods, arguing that the wildest excesses cause more pain than they relieve. Only fragments and a few complete letters of his vast output survive, mostly preserved by later followers rather than in his own manuscripts.

Erasmus was born in Rotterdam in 1466, the illegitimate son of a priest, a fact he spent much of his life quietly obscuring in an era when it could have barred him from clerical office. He was educated by the Brethren of the Common Life before entering an Augustinian monastery he later left, never comfortable inside an institution he could critique more sharply from outside it.

His 1516 Greek New Testament, assembled from a handful of imperfect manuscripts, exposed places where the Latin Vulgate had drifted from the original text over a thousand years of copying. He intended it as a tool for better Christian scholarship, not a rupture with Rome, and spent his later years disowned by reformers who read his own criticisms as an invitation he never meant to extend.

Hemingway started as a newspaper reporter in Kansas City, where the style sheet banning long sentences and ornate adjectives shaped a prose habit he never really broke. He was badly wounded by mortar fire while volunteering as an ambulance driver in Italy in 1918, an experience he later reworked into A Farewell to Arms.

The Old Man and the Sea, a short novel about a Cuban fisherman's exhausting fight with a marlin, appeared in 1952 after nearly a decade in which critics had written him off. It won the Pulitzer Prize the following year and was cited directly when he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954.

Rutherford was born on a farm near Nelson, New Zealand, in 1871, the fourth of twelve children of a wheelwright. A scholarship took him across the world to Cambridge, where he arrived with a device for detecting radio waves that briefly held a distance record, before Marconi's work overtook it and Rutherford turned to the new subject of radioactivity instead.

His 1908 Nobel Prize, in Chemistry rather than Physics, annoyed him: he considered himself thoroughly a physicist and joked that his transformation into a chemist was the swiftest of his career. That prize came three years before the discovery that made him famous. In 1911, interpreting an odd result from alpha particles fired at gold foil, he worked out that an atom is mostly empty space around a tiny, dense, charged core, the nucleus.

Schrodinger wrote his wave equation in early 1926 during a stay in the Swiss Alps, working, by most accounts of his colleagues, alongside a lover whose identity he never named in his own notes. The equation described particles as spread-out waves of probability rather than points with fixed positions, and it gave physicists a tool that actually predicted experimental results.

He proposed the cat thought experiment in 1935, not to illustrate quantum theory but to mock it: a cat sealed in a box with a radioactive trigger would be, under the theory's own logic, neither alive nor dead until observed. He intended it as an objection. It became the most famous shorthand for the idea he was attacking.

Almost nothing is recorded about Euclid's life beyond that he taught in Alexandria around 300 BCE, probably during the reign of Ptolemy I; even his birthplace is unknown, and later ancient biographies confuse him at points with the earlier philosopher Euclid of Megara.

What survives instead is the Elements, thirteen books building geometry up from a small set of definitions and postulates, a structure so influential that it stayed a standard textbook, with only minor revision, into the twentieth century. Abraham Lincoln reportedly studied it by candlelight to sharpen his legal reasoning, a detail that says more about the book's reach than anything known about the man who wrote it.

Euripides was born around 480 BCE, by tradition on the day of the Battle of Salamis, though ancient biographers liked tidy coincidences and this one may simply be too convenient to trust. He wrote roughly ninety plays across a long career, of which nineteen survive, more than any other Greek tragedian, largely by chance of manuscript survival rather than ancient acclaim.

His Athenian audiences found him unsettling: he gave female and enslaved characters extended reasoning voices, questioned the gods' justice openly, and was mocked by Aristophanes for it in comedy performed in his own lifetime. He left Athens near the end of his life for the Macedonian court, where he died, reportedly, before finishing his final play.

Fitzgerald was born in St Paul, Minnesota, and dropped out of Princeton without a degree before selling his first novel, This Side of Paradise, at 23. Its success in 1920 let him marry Zelda Sayre, who had turned him down for lack of money, and the two became fixtures of the wealthy, restless circles he wrote about.

The Great Gatsby sold poorly on its 1925 release and Fitzgerald died in 1940 believing himself a failure, his books mostly out of print. It was reissued to American soldiers during the Second World War and only became a fixture of school curricula and the label 'the great American novel' well after his death.

Fidel Castro was born on 13 August 1926 near Biran, Cuba, the son of a wealthy sugar plantation owner, and trained as a lawyer before turning to armed rebellion against Fulgencio Batista's government. His first attack, on the Moncada army barracks in 1953, failed and landed him in prison, where he gave a courtroom speech later published as History Will Absolve Me.

He landed back in Cuba in 1956 with fewer than one hundred fighters aboard the yacht Granma and took Havana just over two years later, on 1 January 1959. He ruled Cuba for nearly five decades, nationalising industry and aligning with the Soviet Union, survived a US-backed invasion at the Bay of Pigs in 1961, and ceded power to his brother Raul in 2006 due to illness.

Francis was born Giovanni di Pietro di Bernardone in 1181 or 1182 in Assisi, the son of a wealthy cloth merchant. His father's trade with France earned him the nickname Francesco, and he was raised for a life of business, not devotion. A spell as a prisoner of war after a local battle, followed by a serious illness, is the point most accounts trace his change of direction to.

He gave up his inheritance publicly, reportedly stripping off his clothes in front of his father and the local bishop, and began living among lepers and beggars around 1206. The order he founded took vows of poverty that Francis meant literally: friars were forbidden to own property even collectively, a rule strict enough that disputes over relaxing it split the Franciscans for centuries after his death in 1226.

Francis Bacon was born in London in 1561, the son of a senior officeholder under Elizabeth I, and trained as a lawyer before building a political career that eventually made him Lord Chancellor under James I. That career ended in disgrace in 1621, when Parliament found him guilty of accepting bribes from litigants in cases before him, a charge he did not seriously contest.

His lasting influence came from his writing on method rather than his politics: works like the Novum Organum argued that knowledge should be built from careful observation and controlled experiment rather than from received authority or abstract reasoning. He died in 1626, reportedly after catching a chill while testing whether snow could preserve meat, a detail repeated often enough that it has become difficult to separate from legend.

Francis Drake was born around 1540 in Devon, one of a dozen children of a Protestant preacher whose family fled to Kent during a Catholic uprising when Drake was still young. He went to sea early, apprenticed to a shipmaster who left him a small vessel of his own on his death.

Drake's circumnavigation of the globe between 1577 and 1580, undertaken partly to raid Spanish ports and ships along the Pacific coast of the Americas, made him wealthy enough that Elizabeth I knighted him aboard his own ship, the Golden Hind. In 1588 he was a vice admiral against the Spanish Armada, though Spanish accounts of that campaign, unsurprisingly, remember him rather less fondly than English ones do.

Francisco Pizarro was born around 1478 in Trujillo, Spain, an illegitimate son who never learned to read or write and spent his early years tending pigs before leaving for the Americas as a soldier of fortune. He arrived with no fortune and little standing, building his reputation slowly over two decades of expeditions along the Pacific coast of South America.

In 1532 he captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca after a brief, one-sided confrontation, then had him executed the following year despite a ransom in gold and silver already paid. Pizarro founded Lima in 1535 as the new colonial capital, but the conquest he led fractured almost immediately into civil war among the Spanish themselves, and he was assassinated by rival conquistadors in 1541.

Frank Lloyd Wright was born on 8 June 1867 in Richland Center, Wisconsin, and later claimed a birth year of 1869, a discrepancy historians attribute to his lifelong habit of shaping his own legend. He trained briefly in engineering before apprenticing under Chicago architect Louis Sullivan, whose credo that form should follow function stayed with him even as his own style diverged sharply from his teacher's.

Wright designed Fallingwater, a house cantilevered over a waterfall in rural Pennsylvania, in 1935 for the Kaufmann family, and it became the building most associated with his idea of organic architecture, structures grown from their setting rather than imposed on it. Over a roughly seventy-year career he designed more than a thousand structures, of which about half were actually built.

Frank Sinatra was born on 12 December 1915 in Hoboken, New Jersey, delivered with forceps in a birth so difficult that he carried scars on his face and ear for life. He learned much of his phrasing from watching trombonist Tommy Dorsey control breath across long musical lines, then adapted the trick to singing lyrics in a single unbroken phrase.

By the early 1940s, bobby-soxers were fainting and screaming at his shows years before the term teen idol existed for anyone else. His career nearly collapsed by 1952 as his voice weakened and his record label dropped him, then recovered when he won an Academy Award for a dramatic, non-singing role in From Here to Eternity the following year.

Kafka was born in Prague in 1883 into a German-speaking Jewish family, and worked for most of his adult life at an insurance institute, writing fiction largely at night after long days assessing workplace accident claims. He published only a handful of stories in his lifetime and considered most of his work unfinished or unworthy of print.

He instructed his friend Max Brod to burn his unpublished manuscripts after his death in 1924, including the novels The Trial and The Castle, and Brod edited and published them anyway. The Metamorphosis, in which a travelling salesman wakes transformed into a giant insect and finds his family's disgust matters more than the transformation itself, gave literary criticism the term Kafkaesque.

Franz Schubert was born in a Vienna suburb on 31 January 1797, one of only five of his parents' fourteen children to survive infancy. He trained as a choirboy and briefly as a schoolteacher like his father before giving it up to write music full time, a decision that left him poor for most of his short life.

He wrote at a pace few composers have matched, producing hundreds of songs, symphonies, and chamber works in barely fifteen working years, sometimes several finished pieces in a single day. Almost none of it made him money; the Unfinished Symphony sat unperformed in a drawer for decades. He died in Vienna in 1828 at thirty one, probably of typhoid fever, and asked to be buried near Beethoven, whose funeral he had helped carry the year before.

Freddie Mercury was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town, Zanzibar, in 1946, to Parsi parents whose families had migrated from India generations earlier. He was sent to boarding school near Bombay as a child, where he first played in a band, before rejoining his family in England in 1964 after Zanzibar's revolution forced them to leave.

He studied graphic design in London and designed Queen's crest logo himself, combining the zodiac signs of the four band members around a phoenix. His four-octave range and stage presence were matched by chronic stage fright over his teeth, which he never had corrected because he believed the extra space in his mouth contributed to his voice.

Frederic Chopin was born near Warsaw in 1810, likely on 1 March though the exact date is disputed even in his own family's records, to a French father and a Polish mother. He was performing publicly by the age of eight and left Poland for good in 1830, just weeks before an uprising against Russian rule broke out there, a departure he came to treat as permanent exile rather than a trip abroad.

He settled in Paris and made his living largely through teaching and small salon performances rather than large public concerts, which he found draining. His relationship with the writer George Sand, who published under a male pen name, lasted roughly a decade. He died of tuberculosis in Paris in 1849 and, at his own request, had his heart removed and smuggled to Warsaw, where it remains sealed inside a church pillar.

Douglass never knew his exact birth date. Born enslaved in Talbot County, Maryland, around February 1818, he later chose 14 February as the day to celebrate, since his mother had once called him her little valentine. He taught himself to read partly through a white boy he traded bread for lessons with, work slaveholders considered dangerous.

He escaped north in 1838 disguised as a sailor, using papers borrowed from a free Black seaman. His 1845 memoir was so specific about names and places that friends worried it would let his old owner recapture him, so he spent two years lecturing in Britain before it was safe to return. He later advised Lincoln and recruited Black soldiers for the Union Army.

Kahlo had already survived childhood polio when, at eighteen, the bus she was riding collided with a streetcar and a metal handrail impaled her through the pelvis. She spent months in a full body cast and endured over thirty operations across her life, and she began painting seriously during the long recovery, working from a bed fitted with a mirror above it.

She married the muralist Diego Rivera in 1929 in a relationship both of them repeatedly betrayed, including her own affair with the exiled Leon Trotsky while he lived in her family's Mexico City home. Her small, intensely detailed self-portraits, many painted directly from that bedside mirror, went largely unrecognised by the wider art world until decades after her death in 1954.

Dostoevsky was born in Moscow in 1821 and, as a young writer, was arrested for belonging to a discussion circle that read banned political texts. In 1849 he stood before a firing squad with other members, and only after the rifles were raised did an officer arrive with a message commuting the sentence to Siberian exile, a reprieve staged in advance by the tsar himself.

He spent four years in a Siberian labour camp and more in military service before returning to writing. Chronic gambling debts, not literary ambition, forced him to dictate Crime and Punishment against a punishing deadline in the 1860s. He died in St Petersburg in 1881, having finished The Brothers Karamazov only months earlier.

Galileo Galilei was born in Pisa in 1564 and initially studied medicine before switching to mathematics, a shift his father resisted because it offered far less certain income. He did not invent the telescope, which had already appeared in the Netherlands, but he improved its design and turned it toward the sky with unusual persistence.

Through it he saw craters on the Moon, four moons orbiting Jupiter, and phases of Venus that made sense only if Venus circled the Sun, evidence that publicly supported Copernicus's model. The Catholic Church's Inquisition tried him for heresy in 1633 and forced a recantation; he spent his remaining years under house arrest, still working, going blind before his death in 1642.

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel was born in Stuttgart in 1770 and spent years as a private tutor and newspaper editor before finally landing a university post in his forties, publishing his major early work, The Phenomenology of Spirit, in 1807 while Napoleon's army occupied Jena.

His idea that history moves through conflict and resolution, thesis meeting its opposite and producing something new, gave later thinkers a framework they turned to very different ends. Karl Marx inverted Hegel's idealism into a materialist theory of class struggle, while other readers drew existentialist and conservative lessons from the same texts.

George H. W. Bush was born on 12 June 1924 in Milton, Massachusetts, into a wealthy banking family, and enlisted in the navy on his eighteenth birthday. He became one of its youngest pilots and was shot down over the Pacific in 1944, spending hours in a life raft before a submarine rescued him.

As Ronald Reagan's vice president for eight years, he then won the presidency in 1988 and assembled the international coalition that expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War, a campaign completed in weeks. He also presided over the fall of the Berlin Wall and the Soviet Union's dissolution, though he lost re-election in 1992 to Bill Clinton amid a domestic recession.

Orwell was born Eric Arthur Blair in Motihari, in what was then British India, where his father worked for the opium department of the colonial government. He adopted the pen name George Orwell in 1933, borrowing the surname from a river in Suffolk near where his family had settled, partly to spare his relatives embarrassment over his early, unflattering writing about poverty.

He fought with a socialist militia during the Spanish Civil War and was shot through the throat by a sniper near Huesca in 1937, an injury he survived only because the bullet missed his carotid artery by a few millimetres. Nineteen Eighty-Four, written while he was seriously ill with tuberculosis on the Scottish island of Jura, appeared in 1949, months before his death, and gave English the words Big Brother, doublethink and thought police.

George Washington was born on 22 February 1732 on a Virginia tobacco farm, the eldest son of his father's second marriage. He spent his twenties as a surveyor and militia officer, learning the frontier terrain he would later fight and retreat across as commander of the Continental Army.

Washington lost more battles than he won, but he kept an army together through six winters and refused, twice, to become a king. He set the precedent of a two-term presidency by choice rather than law, a precedent that held for a century and a half until Franklin Roosevelt ran for a third term.

Georges Cuvier was born in 1769 in Montbeliard, then part of Wurttemberg, and worked as a tutor to a noble family in Normandy before securing a post at the Paris Museum of Natural History in 1795, where he made his career dissecting and comparing skeletons rather than living animals.

By matching bone to bone he could describe a whole extinct creature, mammoth, giant sloth or mosasaur, from a handful of fossil fragments, and he argued from that evidence that entire species had once existed and vanished, a claim many naturalists still doubted at the time. That argument for extinction as a real, documented event founded the science of palaeontology and comparative anatomy that followed him.

O'Keeffe grew up on a Wisconsin dairy farm and trained in Chicago and New York before the photographer Alfred Stieglitz, whom she later married, began exhibiting her work in 1916 without asking her first. His gallery framed her flower paintings in sexual terms that she spent much of her career publicly rejecting.

She first visited New Mexico in 1929 and moved there permanently after Stieglitz died in 1946, settling at Ghost Ranch. The bleached animal skulls and adobe walls she painted there through her seventies and eighties came from land she walked and photographed for decades, not from a single visit turned into a signature.

Mendel was born to a peasant farming family in Moravia in 1822 and entered an Augustinian monastery largely because it was one of the few routes to an education he could afford. In the monastery garden at Brno he bred roughly 28,000 pea plants over eight years, tracking traits like flower colour and seed shape across generations to work out how they were inherited.

His 1866 paper describing what became the laws of dominant and recessive traits was barely noticed in his lifetime; he later became abbot and largely stopped his research amid administrative duties and a tax dispute with the state. Only around 1900, after his death, did other scientists rediscover the paper and recognise it as the foundation of genetics.

Marconi was born in Bologna in 1874 to an Italian father and an Irish mother from the Jameson whiskey family, and he built his first working wireless apparatus in an attic, ringing a bell across the room without wires. When the Italian government showed no interest, he took the equipment to Britain instead, where the Post Office backed his experiments.

In 1901 he claimed to have received a signal transmitted across the Atlantic from Cornwall to Newfoundland, a distance many physicists thought impossible given the curve of the earth. He shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Karl Ferdinand Braun, whose circuit improvements had made Marconi's transmitters practical, for work that turned wireless telegraphy into ships' standard equipment within a decade.

Gustav Klimt was born near Vienna on 14 July 1862, the son of a gold engraver, a trade whose material later became his signature: gold leaf worked into paintings like The Kiss and the portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer. He trained not as a painter but as a decorative craftsman, taking commissions to decorate theatres and museums before turning toward fine art.

In 1897 he helped found the Vienna Secession, a group of artists breaking from the conservative academy that controlled what could be exhibited, and he was its first president. A commissioned set of ceiling paintings for the University of Vienna was rejected by faculty as pornographic in 1900, a controversy so bitter that Klimt never again accepted a public commission.

Gustav Mahler was born on 7 July 1860 in Kalischt, Bohemia, into a Jewish family in a region where that meant he could conduct only after converting to Catholicism, a step he took in 1897 to secure the directorship of the Vienna Court Opera. He was already known across Europe as a formidable conductor long before audiences accepted him as a composer of equal weight.

He composed mostly in summer breaks from the podium, building symphonies that could run ninety minutes and require choirs and offstage brass alongside a full orchestra. His Eighth Symphony, premiered in 1910, used over a thousand performers and became known as the Symphony of a Thousand, though Mahler himself thought his music would only be properly understood after his death.

Flaubert was born in Rouen in 1821, the son of a surgeon, and wrote so slowly that he sometimes produced only a page a week, weighing every word aloud before committing to it. Madame Bovary, serialised in 1856, drew a prosecution for offending public morals and religion; Flaubert was acquitted, and the scandal made the book a bestseller once it appeared as a novel.

He rarely left his family's house at Croisset on the Seine, treating writing as a discipline closer to manual labour than inspiration. He coined the ideal of the mot juste, the single exactly right word, and left an unfinished satirical novel, Bouvard et Pecuchet, when he died suddenly in 1880.

Johannes Gutenberg's birth date is not recorded; historians place it around 1400 in Mainz based on a document showing he had reached legal adulthood by 1420. He trained as a goldsmith, a trade that gave him the metalworking skill later needed to cast reusable, uniform type, and he spent years in debt-funded secrecy developing the press before it produced anything.

His workshop's Bible, printed around 1455 in an edition of roughly 180 copies, was not sold as a novelty but priced to compete with hand-copied manuscripts, at a fraction of the labour. A lawsuit from his financial backer, Johann Fust, stripped Gutenberg of his own press and type shortly after, so he died in relative poverty while the technology he built spread across Europe within decades.
