Hadrian was born in 76 CE, likely in Rome to a family from Italica in Spain, and was raised partly under the guardianship of his relative Trajan after his father's early death. He served under Trajan on campaign and was, by disputed accounts, adopted as heir only on Trajan's deathbed in 117 CE, a succession clean enough to invite suspicion that it was arranged after the fact.

Where Trajan had expanded the empire, Hadrian spent much of his reign consolidating it, touring the provinces in person and ordering the construction of a stone and turf wall across northern Britain, begun around 122 CE, to mark and defend a fixed frontier rather than push further north. Substantial stretches of that wall still stand.

George Frideric Handel was born in Halle in the same year as Bach, though the two never met despite living much of their lives within a few hundred miles of each other. Handel moved to London in 1712 and stayed there for the rest of his career, becoming a naturalised British subject and writing in Italian, English and German by turns depending on what the city's audiences wanted.

Messiah was composed in just over three weeks in 1741 and premiered in Dublin the following year as a charity benefit, raising enough money to free over a hundred men from debtors' prison. Handel went blind in his final years, reportedly from cataracts, and continued to conduct performances of his own oratorios from memory almost to the end of his life in 1759.

Hannibal was born in Carthage in 247 BCE to Hamilcar Barca, a general who, according to the historian Livy, made his young son swear an oath of eternal enmity toward Rome before an altar. Whether the oath is fact or later legend, Hannibal spent his career fighting the war it describes.

In 218 BCE he led an army, including a small number of war elephants, across the Alps into Italy, a crossing so costly in men and animals that only a fraction of the elephants survived it. He won major battles at Trebia, Trasimene and Cannae, yet Rome refused to surrender, and Hannibal spent fifteen years campaigning on Italian soil without ever capturing the city itself.

Tubman was born enslaved in Dorchester County, Maryland, around 1822, and suffered a permanent head injury as a teenager when an overseer threw a heavy weight that struck her, causing seizures and sleeping spells for the rest of her life. She escaped alone in 1849, following the North Star largely at night.

Rather than staying free, she went back. Over roughly a decade she made about thirteen trips into Maryland and led an estimated seventy enslaved people, including her own parents, north on the Underground Railroad, never once being caught. During the Civil War she also worked as a Union scout and spy, and in 1863 helped plan a raid that freed more than seven hundred people in South Carolina.

The man born Erik Weisz in Budapest in 1874 grew up poor after his family emigrated to Wisconsin, and he took his stage name from the French magician Robert-Houdin. Early in his career he billed himself as the King of Cards before discovering that escapes drew bigger crowds than sleight of hand, and he built an act around handcuffs, locked trunks and, later, tanks of water.

In his final years he turned his skills toward debunking spiritualist mediums, exposing the tricks fraudulent psychics used to fake contact with the dead, which cost him his friendship with Arthur Conan Doyle, a committed believer. Houdini died in 1926 from an infection following a ruptured appendix, an injury he initially dismissed as a bruise from a punch a student had thrown into his stomach.

Truman was born in Lamar, Missouri, in 1884, and unlike most presidents never attended college, working instead as a farmer, bank clerk and shopkeeper before a failed haberdashery business left him paying off debts for years. He entered politics through Kansas City's Pendergast machine and was still a relatively obscure senator when Franklin Roosevelt picked him as running mate in 1944.

He had been vice president for only eighty-two days, and had not been told the atomic bomb existed, when Roosevelt's death in April 1945 made him president. Four months later he authorised its use against Hiroshima and Nagasaki, a decision he defended without apparent hesitation for the rest of his life, arguing it had ended the war and avoided a far bloodier invasion of Japan.

No inscription records the day Hatshepsut was born, only the reign into which she was born, around 1507 BCE, as a daughter of Thutmose I. What survives instead is the record she built later: statues, temple reliefs and inscriptions at Deir el-Bahari recut, decades after her death, to show a king rather than a queen who ruled as one.

Her throne name, Maatkare, appears on obelisks and on trade expedition texts describing voyages to Punt for incense and ivory. Officials writing about her sometimes used male grammatical forms, sometimes female, an inconsistency historians now read less as confusion than as evidence of a court working out how to describe a woman holding a role every text assumed was male.

Keller was born in Alabama in 1880 with her sight and hearing intact, and lost both before she turned two, likely to an illness such as meningitis or scarlet fever. For years afterward she communicated through crude signs and tantrums of frustration, until her family hired Anne Sullivan, a twenty-year-old graduate of the Perkins School for the Blind, when Keller was six.

Sullivan's breakthrough came at a water pump, spelling w-a-t-e-r into Keller's hand as the water ran over it, the moment Keller later described as the one that gave her language. She went on to graduate from Radcliffe College in 1904, wrote a dozen books, and worked for decades as a campaigner for disabled people and for causes including workers' rights and women's suffrage.

Henri Matisse was born on 31 December 1869 in Le Cateau-Cambresis in northern France, and originally trained as a lawyer, only turning to painting after a bout of appendicitis left him bedridden and his mother gave him a paintbox to pass the time. He later called that recovery the moment he found what he wanted to do with his life.

At the 1905 Salon d'Automne in Paris, Matisse and a group of painters using violently unnatural colour were dismissed by a critic as fauves, or wild beasts, giving the movement its name. Matisse kept experimenting into old age, and when illness in his final years made painting difficult he turned to cut paper, producing large works of pure colour shapes he assembled by hand.

Thoreau was born in Concord, Massachusetts, in 1817, and he barely left it. He spent two years in a cabin he built on Ralph Waldo Emerson's land by Walden Pond, not as a hermit but a few kilometres from town, walking home for dinner and newspapers. The point was not isolation, it was seeing how little a person actually needs.

Civil Disobedience grew out of a night in jail in 1846 for refusing to pay a poll tax that funded a war with Mexico he opposed. The essay later reached Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr., who both credited it directly. Thoreau died of tuberculosis in 1862, at 44, having published only two books in his lifetime.

Henry Ford was born on 30 July 1863 on a farm near Dearborn, Michigan, and disliked farm work enough that he spent his boyhood taking apart watches and machinery instead. He founded the Ford Motor Company in 1903 after two earlier ventures had failed, and the Model T followed in 1908 as a car built to be simple and cheap enough for a farmhand to own.

In 1913 Ford installed a moving assembly line at his Highland Park plant, cutting the time to build a Model T from over twelve hours to about ninety minutes. He also raised his workers' minimum pay to five dollars a day in 1914, roughly double the going rate, reasoning that better-paid workers would buy more of what they built.

Hernan Cortes was born in Medellin, Spain, in 1485, to a family of minor hidalgo status without great wealth, and briefly studied law before abandoning it for the Americas at nineteen. He spent over a decade establishing himself in Cuba before the governor there authorised his expedition to Mexico in 1519, a commission Cortes then defied by pushing further inland than instructed.

He reached the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan and, after an initial alliance turned violent, besieged and destroyed the city in 1521 with help from tens of thousands of indigenous allies hostile to Aztec rule, particularly the Tlaxcalans. The victory owed as much to that coalition and to smallpox spreading through the besieged city as to Spanish arms, a balance later retellings often flattened into personal conquest.

Herodotus was born around 484 BCE in Halicarnassus, a Greek city then under Persian control, which may explain why he wrote about the Persian side with more curiosity than contempt. He travelled widely across Egypt, Persia and the Black Sea coast, describing customs, geography and monuments he claimed to have seen firsthand.

Cicero later called him the father of history, but the title came with a rival nickname too: Aristotle and others accused him of being the father of lies, for reporting griffins guarding gold and men with dogs' heads alongside sober military detail. Modern archaeology has since confirmed enough of his geography and customs to rehabilitate much, though not all, of his reputation.

No fact about Homer's birth is secure enough to state as fact. Ancient sources disagree on his home city, name a dozen candidates from Smyrna to Chios, and disagree on his era by centuries; Herodotus put him around 850 BCE, others earlier. The date used here, around 800 BCE, is a convention, not a record.

What survives is the poetry, transmitted orally for generations before being fixed in writing, and a scholarly argument that has run since the eighteenth century over whether one person composed the Iliad and the Odyssey at all, or whether Homer is the name later editors gave to a tradition of many poets. The uncertainty is itself the oldest fact about him.

Stravinsky was born near St Petersburg in 1882, the son of an opera singer, and came to international attention through a string of ballets written for Sergei Diaghilev's company in Paris, starting with The Firebird in 1910. He was still in his twenties when those commissions made him famous across Europe.

The premiere of The Rite of Spring in 1913 is said to have caused a near riot in the theatre, provoked by Nijinsky's angular choreography as much as by Stravinsky's dissonant, irregularly accented score depicting a pagan sacrifice. He later moved away from that raw style toward a cooler, more structured neoclassicism, and after settling in the United States he experimented with serial techniques associated with composers he had once rivalled.

Immanuel Kant reportedly never travelled more than about ninety miles from Konigsberg, the city where he was born, taught and died, and locals were said to set their clocks by his daily walk, which he took at the same hour regardless of weather. He published almost nothing of major importance until his late fifties, when the Critique of Pure Reason appeared in 1781.

The book tried to work out what the mind can know given the limits of the senses, arguing that space and time are not properties of the world itself but structures the mind imposes on experience. It found few readers at first; Kant later rewrote large sections for a second edition in 1787, still convinced the argument mattered more than the difficulty of the prose carrying it.

Isaac Asimov was born around 2 January 1920 in Petrovichi, in what was then Soviet Russia; his family never recorded the exact date, and he chose one himself after emigrating to Brooklyn as a small child. He trained as a biochemist and taught at Boston University while writing fiction on the side, eventually publishing faster than most full-time novelists.

In a 1942 short story he formulated three laws robots must obey, ranked so that protecting a human always outranks obeying an order, which outranks self-preservation, a hierarchy later writers borrowed and argued with for decades. He wrote or edited close to five hundred books across science fiction, popular science and reference works, and is one of very few authors with volumes in nearly every category of the Dewey Decimal System.

Ivan IV was born in 1530 and became Grand Prince of Moscow at three, after his father's death, growing up amid factional violence between rival noble families that he later said had left him orphaned in all but name. He was crowned Tsar of All Russia in 1547 at sixteen, the first Muscovite ruler to formally take that title rather than the older 'grand prince'.

His reign expanded Russian territory into the Volga region and Siberia, but it is remembered chiefly for the Oprichnina, a private police apparatus he created in 1565 that terrorised the nobility and burned the city of Novgorod in a massacre of thousands. In a fit of rage in 1581 he struck and fatally wounded his own son and heir, an act that left the succession, and much of the dynasty's future, in disarray.

London was born in San Francisco in 1876, likely illegitimate, and left school young to work in a cannery, as an oyster pirate and later as a sailor before joining the Klondike gold rush of 1897. He found almost no gold, but the roughly year he spent in the Yukon supplied the material for the fiction that made him one of the highest paid writers in America.

The Call of the Wild, published in 1903, follows a dog stolen from a California home and sold into the brutal work of the Alaskan sled trade, and it sold rapidly enough to establish him overnight. He wrote prolifically and often carelessly for money afterward, publishing dozens of books before his death in 1916 at forty, and White Fang, in 1906, effectively reversed the first book's arc, following a wild wolf-dog toward domestication.

Jackie Robinson was born on 31 January 1919 in Cairo, Georgia, the grandson of enslaved people, and grew up mostly in Pasadena, California, after his family moved north when he was a toddler. Before baseball he lettered in four sports at UCLA and was an army lieutenant, where he was court-martialled, and acquitted, for refusing to move to the back of a military bus.

Brooklyn Dodgers executive Branch Rickey signed him in 1945 specifically for his ability to withstand abuse without retaliating on the field, a condition Robinson agreed to for his rookie season. He debuted for the Dodgers on 15 April 1947, breaking a colour line that had held in the major leagues for six decades, and endured death threats, beanballs and opposing players who refused to take the field against him.

Jackson Pollock was born on 28 January 1912 in Cody, Wyoming, the youngest of five brothers in a family that moved often for his father's farming and surveying work. He trained as a figurative painter under Thomas Hart Benton in New York before abandoning the easel altogether in the late 1940s.

Pollock laid his canvases flat on the floor of a converted barn on Long Island and worked around them with sticks, trowels and turkey basters, flinging house paint rather than mixing it with a brush. Critics called it action painting, a record of the artist's movement rather than a picture of anything. He died in a car crash in 1956, at 44, on a road near his own studio.

Cousteau built the aqua-lung in 1943 with engineer Emile Gagnan, adapting a demand regulator Gagnan had designed for cooking gas during wartime fuel shortages so that a diver drew a breath only when needed. Cousteau tested it himself in a freezing river outside Paris before taking it into the Mediterranean, where he, Philippe Tailliez and Frederic Dumas logged hundreds of dives that year alone.

He later converted a former British minesweeper, the Calypso, into a floating laboratory and film studio, and his television series brought coral reefs and shipwrecks into homes that had never seen underwater footage before. He also helped design an early underwater camera housing and an early electric submersible, work that shaped ocean conservation as much as popular science television.

Joyce was born in Dublin in 1882 into a once comfortable family whose finances collapsed through his father's drinking and mismanagement, a decline that shadows his fiction throughout. He left Ireland as a young man and spent most of his adult life on the continent, in Trieste, Zurich and Paris, writing almost obsessively about the city he had abandoned.

Ulysses, set entirely on a single day in Dublin in 1904, was serialised, banned for obscenity in both Britain and the United States, and not published legally there until a 1933 court ruling. Its stream of consciousness technique, following characters' thoughts in something close to their raw, unedited form, changed what novelists thought a sentence could be asked to do.

James Watt was born in Greenock, Scotland, in 1736 and trained as an instrument maker before a repair job on a model Newcomen steam engine at Glasgow University showed him how wasteful the design was. Newcomen's engine cooled and reheated the same cylinder on every stroke, burning fuel to no purpose.

Watt's fix, patented in 1769, added a separate condenser so the cylinder stayed hot, roughly doubling the engine's fuel efficiency. He struggled for years to build it reliably before partnering with the manufacturer Matthew Boulton, and the Boulton and Watt engine went on to pump mines and drive the first factory machinery of the Industrial Revolution.

Jane Austen was born in 1775 in Hampshire, one of eight children of a country clergyman, and wrote her early drafts within a busy, book-filled household rather than in any special solitude, at a small writing desk in the family's shared sitting room.

She published anonymously, as 'A Lady', because novel writing was not considered a respectable trade for a gentlewoman, and none of her books carried her name during her lifetime. Pride and Prejudice began as an earlier draft called First Impressions, rejected by a publisher in 1797, and was rewritten and finally published in 1813.

Sartre lost sight in his right eye to a childhood illness, leaving it permanently wandering, a detail he wrote about with the same unsparing honesty he brought to his philosophy. He was captured by German forces in 1940 and spent nine months in a prisoner of war camp, where he read Heidegger and staged his own play for fellow prisoners using a torch for stage lighting.

In 1964 he became the first person to voluntarily decline the Nobel Prize in Literature, writing that a writer should not let himself be turned into an institution, and that he had already refused France's Legion of Honour for the same reason. His letter arrived in Stockholm after the committee had already announced him as its choice, so the award stands on the record as declined rather than never given.

Jimi Hendrix was born in Seattle in 1942 and taught himself guitar partly on a one-string ukulele his father found, before getting his first real guitar at fifteen from an uncle. He served briefly in the US Army as a paratrooper in the early 1960s, an assignment his commanding officers reportedly found he treated with little enthusiasm, and was discharged after about a year.

He spent years as a backing guitarist for touring soul and R&B acts, including Little Richard and the Isley Brothers, before a London manager, Chas Chandler of the Animals, spotted him in a New York club in 1966 and brought him to England. It was there, backed by two British musicians as the Jimi Hendrix Experience, that he built the reputation that made him a headliner at Woodstock within three years.

Brahms was born in Hamburg in 1833, the son of a double bass player, and earned money as a teenager playing piano in the city's dockside taverns. He did not complete his First Symphony until 1876, when he was in his early forties, having spent roughly two decades hesitant to publish one at all under the shadow of Beethoven's reputation.

A conductor later joked that the symphony's finale so echoed Beethoven's Ninth that it deserved the nickname Beethoven's Tenth. Brahms also composed the German Requiem after his mother's death, setting German biblical texts rather than the traditional Latin Mass. He died in Vienna in 1897, less than a year after his close friend Clara Schumann.

John Adams was born in 1735 on a Massachusetts farm and trained as a lawyer, a choice that put him, unusually, on the unpopular side of a famous case: he defended the British soldiers charged after the Boston Massacre and won most of them acquittals. He argued that a fair trial mattered more than the crowd's anger.

He went on to nominate Washington to lead the army, draft much of the case for independence with Jefferson, and serve as the first vice president and second president. He and Jefferson, allies turned rivals turned late-life correspondents, died on the same day, 4 July 1826, exactly fifty years after the Declaration.

John Calvin was born in Noyon, France, in 1509 and trained first in law, not theology, at his father's insistence, before a religious crisis in his mid twenties turned him toward the Reformation. He fled France for Protestant Switzerland as royal pressure on reformers hardened, settling eventually in Geneva.

His Institutes of the Christian Religion, first published in 1536 and expanded across several later editions, laid out predestination as a central doctrine: that salvation was determined by God in advance, not earned. Calvin governed Geneva's religious life with an authority that extended into civic law, and the church discipline he built there became the model for Reformed and Presbyterian churches across Europe.

John Davison Rockefeller was born on 8 July 1839 in Richford, New York, the son of a con man who sold fake cancer cures and sometimes went by an alias to dodge the law. The contrast with his own career was total: Rockefeller kept detailed ledgers from his teenage years and treated bookkeeping almost as a moral practice, a habit that outlasted every business he built.

He entered the oil business in Cleveland in the 1860s and, through Standard Oil, controlled roughly 90 percent of American refining by the 1880s by buying out or undercutting rivals one region at a time. The federal government broke the company into 34 pieces in 1911 under antitrust law, and several of those fragments, including what became ExxonMobil and Chevron, grew large enough on their own to rank among the world's biggest corporations.

John Locke trained as a physician before he became a philosopher, and it was medicine, not politics, that got him close to power: he treated the Earl of Shaftesbury for a liver abscess and became his personal doctor and secretary. Locke's Two Treatises of Government, published anonymously in 1689, argued that legitimate rulers govern only with the consent of the people they rule.

He spent years in exile in the Netherlands after Shaftesbury's political fortunes collapsed, and did not put his name to the Two Treatises until near the end of his life. The ideas travelled further than his caution did. Jefferson leaned on Locke's language of natural rights when drafting the American Declaration of Independence nearly a century later.

Keynes was born in Cambridge in 1883, the son of an economics lecturer, and worked at the Treasury during the First World War before resigning from the British delegation at the Paris peace talks in disgust at the reparations imposed on Germany, warning in print that they would wreck Europe's economy.

His central book, The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money, published in 1936, argued that economies could get stuck with high unemployment unless governments stepped in to spend, rather than waiting for markets to correct themselves. That argument, built on his view that Britain's return to the gold standard in the 1920s had deepened unemployment, reshaped how postwar governments saw their job in a downturn.

Karol Wojtyla was born on 18 May 1920 in Wadowice, Poland, and lost his mother, brother and father by the time he was 20. He worked in a stone quarry and a chemical plant under Nazi occupation, partly to avoid deportation for forced labour, while studying for the priesthood in secret seminary classes banned by the regime.

Elected pope in October 1978, he was the first non-Italian in 455 years and the first ever from a communist-controlled country. His 1979 return to Poland as pope drew crowds in the millions and is widely credited with emboldening the Solidarity trade union movement that helped end communist rule there a decade later. He survived an assassination attempt in Rome's St Peter's Square in 1981.

Steinbeck grew up in the Salinas Valley among the ranch hands and migrant labourers who later filled his novels, and he worked alongside them as a young man on ranches and in a sugar factory before he could afford to write full time. The Grapes of Wrath, published in 1939, followed one displaced family north from the Dust Bowl to California, and drew on articles Steinbeck had written about migrant labour camps for a San Francisco newspaper.

The novel was banned and publicly burned in some California counties, where growers objected to its portrayal of how migrant workers were treated. It won the Pulitzer Prize in 1940 and was cited directly when Steinbeck received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1962, a choice some critics at the time thought had come decades after his best work.

Von Neumann was born in Budapest and could reportedly divide two eight-digit numbers in his head as a child, a memory and speed that colleagues at Princeton's Institute for Advanced Study never stopped mentioning decades later. He earned a chemical engineering degree alongside a doctorate in mathematics, apparently to satisfy his father that mathematics alone was not a living.

During the Manhattan Project he worked out the explosive lens design that let the plutonium bomb compress evenly, and that work fed into the architecture he later designed for early digital computers, including the stored-program layout still called the von Neumann architecture. He also helped formalise game theory with economist Oskar Morgenstern in a 1944 book that reshaped how economists modelled decisions under conflict.

Borges grew up bilingual in Buenos Aires, reading Cervantes in English translation before he read it in Spanish, and spent much of his career working as a municipal librarian rather than a professor. A hereditary eye condition left him effectively blind by the 1950s, and from then on he composed by dictation, never writing anything long enough to need a chapter break.

His stories, collected in Ficciones and El Aleph, invent libraries that contain every possible book and maps as large as the territories they describe, treating ideas from logic and theology as material for fiction rather than argument. He never wrote a novel, insisting the short story was the form that could hold an idea without diluting it.

Joseph Conrad was born Jozef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski on 4 December 1857 in Berdychiv, then part of the Russian Empire and now in Ukraine, to Polish parents exiled for nationalist activity. Both his parents died of tuberculosis before he was twelve, and he went to sea at seventeen, first in the French merchant marine and then the British, before earning his master mariner's certificate and British citizenship in 1886.

He did not begin writing in English, his third language after Polish and French, until his thirties, drawing on an 1890 trip up the Congo River as a steamboat officer that became the basis for Heart of Darkness. The novella, published in 1899, examined the brutality of Belgian colonial rule through a narrator's account, and its ambiguity toward that narrator has kept it a subject of argument since.

Joseph Haydn was born in 1732 in the Austrian village of Rohrau, the son of a wheelwright, and left home at six to sing as a chorister in Vienna. He spent nearly three decades in the isolated service of the Esterhazy princes, where he had an orchestra to experiment on and almost no audience to please.

That isolation is credited with shaping the classical symphony and string quartet as we know them; he wrote well over a hundred symphonies and dozens of quartets, effectively working out the forms by trial. Mozart called him his teacher, and Beethoven took lessons from him briefly in Vienna in the early 1790s.

Tolkien was born in Bloemfontein in the Orange Free State, where his father worked for a British bank, and was brought back to England at three after his father died; he never returned to South Africa. He fought at the Somme in 1916, and of the close friends who formed his schoolboy literary club, only he and one other survived the war.

He built Middle-earth's languages before its stories, inventing Elvish grammars as an Oxford philologist's private hobby and then writing The Hobbit in 1937 partly to give the invented world somewhere to live. The Lord of the Rings, begun as its sequel, took another seventeen years to finish and publish.

Verne was born in Nantes in 1828 and, as a boy, reportedly tried to run away to sea on a ship bound for the Indies, only to be caught by his father before it left port. He trained as a lawyer to satisfy his family before turning to writing full time.

His publisher, Pierre-Jules Hetzel, pushed him toward adventure fiction grounded in real science, a combination that produced Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea and Around the World in Eighty Days. Verne researched submarines, ballooning and lunar mechanics closely enough that later engineers, including submarine designers, credited his novels as an influence. He died in Amiens in 1905.

Justinian was born Petrus Sabbatius in 482 in Tauresium, a village in the province of Dardania in what is now North Macedonia. He was a peasant's nephew, not a noble: his uncle Justin, an army officer who rose through the ranks to become emperor, brought him to Constantinople, adopted him and had him educated for the throne he would inherit in 527.

The Corpus Juris Civilis that carries his name was not his own drafting. He commissioned the jurist Tribonian to compile and reconcile centuries of contradictory Roman law into a single code, finished within about six years. Justinian also rebuilt the Hagia Sophia after riots burned the earlier church, and briefly retook Italy and North Africa, wars that emptied the treasury faster than they secured the reconquest.

Marx was born in Trier in 1818 into a family that had converted from Judaism to Lutheranism a few years earlier, a move his lawyer father made to keep his career open under Prussian law. Marx spent much of his adult life stateless, expelled from Prussia, France and Belgium in turn for his politics before settling in London in 1849.

He never held a university post after his student years and relied heavily on his friend and co-author Friedrich Engels, a factory owner's son, to pay his debts. Only the first volume of Das Kapital was finished before he died in 1883; Engels edited the remaining two from Marx's notes. He is buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Hepburn wore trousers in public in an era when that alone drew press criticism, and by the late 1930s a trade publication had labelled her box office poison after a run of commercial flops. She responded by buying out her own studio contract and choosing The Philadelphia Story, a play written for her, as a stage comeback that Hollywood then had to bid for.

She won four Academy Awards for Best Actress, still the record, spread across five decades from Morning Glory in 1934 to On Golden Pond in 1981. Her decades-long partnership with Spencer Tracy, on screen in nine films and off screen for years, was kept largely out of the press even though he never divorced his wife.

Johannes Kepler grew up in a household his own mother's neighbours later swore was cursed. In 1615, when Katharina Kepler was in her late sixties, women in the town of Leonberg accused her of poisoning a neighbour, crippling a man by touch, and turning herself into a cat. Kepler, by then imperial mathematician to Rudolf II, took over her legal defence himself.

The case dragged on for six years while Kepler picked apart the testimony, arguing that the illnesses blamed on witchcraft had ordinary medical explanations. Katharina was held in chains for fourteen months before a court finally cleared her, though ill will in Leonberg meant she could never move back. She died within six months of her release, while her son continued refining the planetary laws that carry his name.

Kobe Bryant was born in Philadelphia in 1978, the son of former NBA player Joe Bryant, and spent part of his childhood in Italy while his father played professionally there, which is where he learned to speak Italian fluently. He entered the NBA draft directly from high school in 1996 and was picked 13th before being traded to the Lakers on draft night.

He won three championships alongside Shaquille O'Neal in the early 2000s and two more after a public and difficult split from him, scoring 81 points in a single game in 2006, the second-highest total in NBA history. He retired in 2020 having also won an Academy Award for an animated short film he wrote, and died in a helicopter crash later that year alongside his daughter Gianna and seven others.

Kublai was born in 1215, a grandson of Genghis Khan, and grew up in a Mongol court still consolidating an empire that stretched from China to Eastern Europe. He was not the eldest of his generation and only secured the position of Great Khan in 1260 after a civil war against his own brother Ariq Boke, fought over who would succeed their brother Mongke.

Ruling China meant adapting rather than imposing Mongol custom: Kublai took a Chinese dynastic name, Yuan, moved the capital to a new city near modern Beijing, and employed foreign administrators, including for a time the Venetian Marco Polo, precisely because he distrusted handing power to the Chinese gentry his conquest had displaced. Two attempted invasions of Japan, in 1274 and 1281, both failed after storms destroyed his fleets.

Godel was so anxious about accidental poisoning that for the last years of his life he would eat only food his wife Adele had personally prepared and tasted first. When she was hospitalised in 1977, he largely stopped eating, and he died months later weighing barely thirty kilograms, a death certificate listing malnutrition caused by personality disturbance.

In 1931, at twenty-five, he published his incompleteness theorems, proving that any mathematical system powerful enough to describe ordinary arithmetic must contain true statements it cannot prove within its own rules. The result unsettled a project mathematicians including David Hilbert had spent decades pursuing, the hope of placing all of mathematics on a single, complete and provably consistent foundation.

The Marquis de Lafayette was born into French nobility in 1757 and orphaned young, inheriting a fortune he used, against his king's wishes, to sail to America and fight for its revolution. He was given a Continental Army command at nineteen and became close to Washington, who treated him almost as a son.

Back in France he pushed for constitutional monarchy rather than the republic that followed, drafting an early version of the Declaration of the Rights of Man before the Revolution turned against moderates like him. He fled the Terror, was imprisoned by the Austrians for five years, and returned to French politics as an old man during the 1830 revolution.

Lao Tzu is traditionally dated to 601 BCE and traditionally identified as a court archivist named Li Er, but the earliest sources that mention him, Sima Qian's history written some four centuries later, already admit uncertainty about whether he was one man or several. No contemporary record of his life exists at all.

The Tao Te Ching itself, the text his name is attached to, likely accreted from multiple contributors over generations rather than arriving from a single hand. Archaeologists found versions of it buried in tombs at Mawangdui and Guodian, centuries apart and differing in wording, which is roughly the closest thing to physical evidence the tradition has.

Tolstoy was born into a wealthy landowning family at Yasnaya Polyana in 1828 and was an artillery officer during the Crimean War, an experience that fed the unsparing battle scenes in War and Peace. He wrote and rewrote that novel so many times that his wife Sophia copied the entire manuscript by hand at least seven times over.

In his fifties he underwent a moral crisis, rejected his own earlier novels as frivolous, and adopted a strict pacifist Christianity that led the Russian Orthodox Church to excommunicate him in 1901. His late writings on nonviolent resistance directly influenced Gandhi, who corresponded with him. Tolstoy died at a remote railway station in 1910 after leaving home in secret.

Carl Linnaeus trained as a physician before botany became his life's work, and he built his classification system partly out of frustration with how inconsistently earlier naturalists named plants. His Systema Naturae, first published in 1735 and expanded over later editions, gave every organism a two-part Latin name, genus and species, that is still the basis of biological naming today.

He sent students on collecting expeditions across the world, several of whom died on the journeys, to bring back specimens he could slot into his system. Linnaeus classified humans within the same framework as other primates, a decision that drew criticism in his own time from those who thought it demeaning, and that later editions of his work revised as attitudes shifted.

George Gordon Byron was born in London on 22 January 1788 with a clubbed foot that caused him lifelong pain and self-consciousness, and he limped through a childhood of debt and an absent father before inheriting the title of sixth Baron Byron at the age of ten from a great-uncle he had barely met.

He woke up famous in 1812, when the first two cantos of Childe Harold's Pilgrimage sold out within days and made him, in his own words, find himself famous overnight. Scandal followed just as fast: a ruinous marriage, rumours of an affair with his half-sister, and mounting debts drove him out of England for good in 1816. He died of fever in 1824 while helping Greek rebels fight for independence from the Ottoman Empire.

Lorenzo de' Medici was born in Florence in 1449, groomed from childhood to inherit the family's informal rule of the city. He took charge of Medici affairs in 1469 at twenty, and survived an assassination attempt in 1478 that killed his brother Giuliano beside him at Mass, an attack backed by a rival family and, controversially, elements of the papacy.

The nickname 'the Magnificent' referred as much to his spending as to his statesmanship: he ran the family bank into decline through poor management even as he funded Botticelli, the young Michelangelo and a revived university, leaving Florence's cultural standing far stronger than its finances by his death in 1492.

Armstrong himself gave his birthday as the Fourth of July, a detail so useful to his own legend that biographers repeated it for decades. His baptismal record, found later, gives the actual date as 4 August 1901, in a poor section of New Orleans he later called the Battlefield. He learned cornet at the Colored Waifs' Home, where he had been sent at eleven for firing a pistol into the air on New Year's Eve.

By the late 1920s his recordings with the Hot Five and Hot Seven reshaped jazz around the improvising soloist rather than the collective ensemble sound that came before him. Tracks like West End Blues showed a level of harmonic daring and rhythmic freedom other trumpeters spent years catching up to, and his gravelly singing voice, first heard widely on Heebie Jeebies, became as influential as his horn playing.

Pasteur was born in Dole, France, in 1822 and trained as a chemist, not a physician, which shaped how he attacked disease: as a contamination problem rather than an imbalance of humours. Studying why wine and beer soured, he showed the culprits were living microorganisms, and that heating a liquid briefly could kill them without ruining the drink, the process now called pasteurisation.

In 1885 he treated a boy bitten by a rabid dog with an experimental vaccine he had only tested on animals, risking prosecution if it failed. The boy survived, and the case built the case for his germ theory of disease. The Pasteur Institute, founded on the resulting fame, still researches infectious disease in Paris.

Wittgenstein was born into one of Vienna's wealthiest families, trained as an aeronautical engineer, and turned to philosophy only after becoming fixated on the foundations of mathematics. He wrote most of his first book, the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, in trenches and an Italian prisoner-of-war camp during the First World War, concluding that language pictures the world and that what cannot be said should be passed over in silence.

After giving away his inherited fortune, he later taught village schoolchildren in rural Austria and worked as a hospital porter in London during the Second World War. His later notes, published after his death as Philosophical Investigations, rejected much of his own earlier book, arguing that meaning comes from how words are used, not from what they picture.

Johnson was sworn in aboard Air Force One on a Dallas runway hours after John F Kennedy's assassination in November 1963, his hand on a Catholic missal because no Bible could be found quickly enough. He had spent decades in Congress mastering the Senate's procedural machinery before becoming, almost by accident, the president who would push through the era's biggest civil rights legislation.

The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965 dismantled the legal architecture of segregation, achievements Johnson knew would cost his own party support in the South for a generation, and told aides so at the time. He escalated American involvement in Vietnam through the same years, and the war's mounting casualties and no clear path to victory drove his approval so low that he declined to seek re-election in 1968.

Niccolo Machiavelli was born in Florence in 1469 to a family of minor gentry with more standing than money. He worked for years as a Florentine diplomat and militia organiser, a career that ended abruptly in 1512 when the Medici retook the city and had him briefly imprisoned and tortured on suspicion of conspiracy.

The Prince, written in exile the following year, was a job application as much as a treatise: Machiavelli dedicated it to Lorenzo de' Medici hoping to win back a post in government. Lorenzo appears to have shown little interest, and Machiavelli never returned to office, dying in 1527 still shut out of the city whose politics he had spent the book dissecting.

Ferdinand Magellan was born around 1480 into minor Portuguese nobility, but it was Spain, not his own king, that funded the westward voyage he proposed to reach the Spice Islands. Portugal's King Manuel had already turned him down, so Magellan sailed under the Spanish flag in 1519 with five ships and a crew that started at roughly 270 men.

Magellan never completed the journey he is remembered for. He was killed in April 1521 in a shallow-water skirmish on Mactan island in the Philippines, wading toward shore against local warriors led by the chief Lapu-Lapu. Command passed to Juan Sebastian Elcano, who brought the single surviving ship, the Victoria, back to Spain in September 1522 with only about eighteen of the original crew aboard.

Marcel Proust was born in the Paris suburb of Auteuil on 10 July 1871, into a wealthy family, and suffered from severe asthma that shaped much of his adult life, eventually confining him largely to a cork-lined bedroom to keep out dust and noise. He spent years as a society figure before turning seriously to the novel that would occupy the rest of his life.

In Search of Lost Time grew to seven volumes and over a million words, published between 1913 and 1927, the last three volumes appearing after Proust's death in 1922. Its opening scene, in which the taste of a tea-soaked madeleine unlocks a flood of childhood memory, gave literary criticism a shorthand term for involuntary memory that outlasted the novel's own reputation for length.

Marco Polo was born in 1254 into a Venetian merchant family already trading as far as the Black Sea. He was seventeen when he set out with his father and uncle on the overland journey to China in 1271, a trip that took roughly three years before they reached Kublai Khan's court.

Most of what is known about his seventeen years in Mongol service comes from a book he did not write himself. Captured by the Genoese after a naval battle in 1298, he dictated his account to a fellow prisoner, a romance writer named Rustichello, and readers for centuries afterward argued over how much of it was travelogue and how much was embellishment.

Marcus Aurelius was born in Rome in 121 CE to a senatorial family, and was singled out for imperial succession as a child by the emperor Hadrian, who arranged for his own successor Antoninus Pius to adopt the boy as heir. He spent decades being groomed for a throne he would not actually hold until 161 CE.

Much of his reign was spent commanding troops on the frontier against Germanic tribes rather than governing from Rome, and the Meditations, the private notebook he is remembered for, was written during those campaigns as personal Stoic exercises never intended for publication. It survived by chance transmission and became one of the most widely read texts of Stoic philosophy only long after his death.

Margaret Thatcher was born Margaret Roberts on 13 October 1925 above her father's grocery shop in Grantham, Lincolnshire, and studied chemistry at Oxford before training as a barrister. She entered Parliament in 1959 and took the Conservative leadership in 1975, unseating the party's sitting leader in a vote few expected her to win.

As prime minister from 1979 she sold off state-owned industries, curbed trade union power after a bitter year-long miners' strike, and sent a naval task force to retake the Falkland Islands from Argentina in 1982. Her monetarist policies cut inflation but drove unemployment above three million, and the moniker Iron Lady, coined by Soviet media as an insult, became one she wore deliberately.

Maria Callas was born on 2 December 1923 in New York City to Greek immigrant parents, George and Evangelia Kalogeropoulos, who shortened the family name after arriving in America. She moved to Athens with her mother at 13 and trained at the Athens Conservatory during the German occupation, singing in productions staged despite wartime shortages.

Her voice was unusually wide-ranging but unevenly coloured across its registers, a flaw some critics attacked and others credited for the raw dramatic force of her acting. She revived long-neglected bel canto roles, particularly Bellini's Norma, at a time opera houses treated them as museum pieces too vocally demanding to stage. Her sound thinned in the 1960s, and she gave her last full opera performance in 1965.

Marie Curie was born Maria Sklodowska in Warsaw on 7 November 1867, at a time when Russian-controlled Poland barred women from university, so she attended a clandestine Flying University before moving to Paris in 1891 to study at the Sorbonne. She met Pierre Curie there in 1894, and their shared research into the intensely radioactive ore pitchblende led them to isolate two new elements, polonium and radium, within a single year.

She shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre and Henri Becquerel, then won a second Nobel, in chemistry, alone in 1911, the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. During the First World War she developed mobile x-ray units, nicknamed petites Curies, and drove them to the front herself to help treat wounded soldiers.

Marilyn Monroe was born Norma Jeane Mortenson on 1 June 1926 in Los Angeles and spent much of her childhood in foster homes and an orphanage while her mother battled mental illness. She began modelling during the Second World War after a photographer spotted her at the aircraft factory where she worked, and signed her first studio contract in 1946.

Twentieth Century-Fox built her into a comic and sexual icon through films like Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, though she pushed for more serious dramatic parts and studied at the Actors Studio in New York. She was found dead in her Los Angeles home on 5 August 1962 of a barbiturate overdose ruled probable suicide, a verdict that decades of retellings have never stopped disputing.

Samuel Clemens was born on 30 November 1835 in Florida, Missouri, two weeks after Halley's Comet passed closest to the sun. He later joked that he came in with the comet and expected to go out with it, and the line held: he died on 21 April 1910, a day after its next perihelion. The dates line up on the calendar even though the comet was not visible from Earth on either exact day.

The pen name came from his years piloting steamboats on the Mississippi, where 'mark twain' was the leadsman's call for two fathoms of water, safe depth for a boat. He took up writing full time after the river trade collapsed with the Civil War, moving through journalism in Nevada and California before Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn made him the country's most quoted humorist.

Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin was born in London on 30 August 1797 to two writers, and her mother, the feminist philosopher Mary Wollstonecraft, died of complications from the birth just eleven days later. She was raised by her father, the political writer William Godwin, who gave her an unusually thorough education for a girl of that era but remarried a stepmother she never got on with.

In the summer of 1816, staying near Geneva with Percy Shelley, Lord Byron and others during an unusually dark, cold summer, the group challenged each other to write ghost stories. Mary's contribution grew into Frankenstein, published anonymously in 1818 when she was twenty. She married Percy Shelley and outlived him by nearly three decades, editing his poems after he drowned in 1822.

Mary Wollstonecraft was born in London in 1759 into a household unsettled by her father's failed ventures and drinking, and she supported herself from her teens as a governess and teacher, publishing her first book, Thoughts on the Education of Daughters, in 1787.

A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, published in 1792, argued that women seemed inferior only because they were denied the same education as men, not because they were naturally so. She died in 1797, days after giving birth to a daughter who grew up to write Frankenstein under the name Mary Shelley.

Max Planck was born on 23 April 1858 in Kiel, then part of Schleswig-Holstein, into a family of lawyers and clergy rather than scientists. He nearly chose music over physics, being a capable pianist and cellist, and later said a professor warned him the field was largely settled and offered little left to discover.

That warning proved wrong within his own lifetime. In December 1900, working on the puzzle of how heated bodies radiate light, Planck proposed that energy is emitted in discrete packets rather than a continuous flow. He called the constant in his equation a mathematical convenience, but it became the foundation of quantum mechanics, and he received the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

Maxwell was born in Edinburgh in 1831 and published his first scientific paper, on drawing perfect ovals with pins and string, at 14. He later showed mathematically that Saturn's rings could not be solid or liquid without breaking apart, and had to be made of countless small particles, a conclusion confirmed more than a century later by spacecraft.

His lasting achievement was showing that electricity, magnetism and light are the same phenomenon, described by a single set of equations, and that light itself is an electromagnetic wave travelling at a speed his own equations predicted. Einstein kept a photograph of Maxwell in his study. Maxwell died of cancer in 1879, at 48, the same disease that had killed his mother at a similar age.

Maya Angelou was born Marguerite Annie Johnson on 4 April 1928 in St. Louis, Missouri, and was sent as a child to live with her grandmother in rural Arkansas, where she experienced the segregation later central to her writing. Before publishing, she worked as a calypso singer, a streetcar conductor in San Francisco, and briefly as a Cairo-based journalist and Ghana-based administrator during the years of African independence movements.

Her first memoir, published in 1969, described a childhood sexual assault with a directness rare in American memoir at the time, and became one of the first bestselling autobiographies by a Black woman. She read her poem On the Pulse of Morning at Bill Clinton's 1993 inauguration, only the second poet ever invited to do so.

Michael Faraday was born in London on 22 September 1791, the son of a blacksmith, and left school at thirteen to work as an errand boy and then an apprentice bookbinder. He read every book that passed through the shop, and a set of lecture tickets given to him by a customer got him into Humphry Davy's talks at the Royal Institution, where he later talked his way into a job washing bottles.

By 1831 Faraday showed that moving a magnet through a coil of wire could generate an electric current. It was a demonstration, not yet a use, and when a minister reportedly asked what good it was, Faraday is said to have answered that he could not say, but one day the man would be able to tax it. He also turned down a knighthood and refused to help Britain make chemical weapons for the Crimean War.

Michelangelo was born in 1475 in Caprese, a small Tuscan village where his father held a minor administrative post, and was sent to a wet nurse whose husband and father were both stonecutters, a detail Michelangelo later joked explained why he loved marble more than paint. He was apprenticed to the painter Domenico Ghirlandaio at thirteen before Lorenzo de' Medici brought him into his household to study sculpture.

He carved the David from a single block of marble that two earlier sculptors had already given up on as flawed and unworkable, finishing it in 1504 at twenty nine. He resented painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling a few years later, considering himself a sculptor pressed into an unfamiliar medium, and complained in letters about the physical toll of working on his back for four years.

Mikhail Gorbachev was born in 1931 in Privolnoye, a village in the North Caucasus, to peasant parents who lived through the famine of the early 1930s that killed millions in the region. He worked alongside his father operating combine harvesters as a teenager and was awarded the Order of the Red Banner of Labour for it before he had finished school, a rare honour for someone so young.

He rose through the Communist Party bureaucracy in agriculture before reaching the Politburo, and became general secretary in 1985 after the two men who held the post before him died within a year of each other. The reforms he introduced, glasnost and perestroika, were meant to renew Soviet socialism rather than end it, but they loosened central control enough that the union he led dissolved within six years.

Mother Teresa was born Anjeze Gonxhe Bojaxhiu to an Albanian family in Skopje, then part of the Ottoman Empire and now the capital of North Macedonia. She travelled to India in 1929 to join the Sisters of Loreto and taught at a Calcutta convent school for nearly two decades before what she described as a call, on a train journey in 1946, to leave and work directly among the city's poorest residents.

She founded the Missionaries of Charity in 1950, which grew from a handful of sisters into a network running hospices, orphanages and clinics across dozens of countries, and she received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979. Critics later questioned the standard of medical care in her hospices, but the Vatican canonized her in September 2016, less than two decades after her death in 1997.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, and his father Leopold, a court musician, began touring him around Europe's courts as a keyboard prodigy before he was six. By his teens he had written symphonies, operas and concertos that adult composers were still struggling to match.

He moved to Vienna as a young man, freelancing rather than serving a single patron, and produced Le Nozze di Figaro, Don Giovanni and The Magic Flute within a few crowded years. He died in 1791 at thirty-five, of an illness never conclusively identified, leaving his Requiem unfinished.

Muhammad Ali was born Cassius Clay in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1942, and started boxing at twelve after a police officer running a local gym suggested it to him following the theft of his bicycle. He won Olympic gold in 1960 and turned professional shortly after, but it was his conversion to the Nation of Islam and his name change in 1964 that set the pattern of his public life.

In 1967 he refused induction into the US Army on religious grounds during the Vietnam War, was stripped of his boxing licence and title, and did not fight again for nearly four years while his conviction was appealed; the Supreme Court overturned it unanimously in 1971. He reclaimed the heavyweight title twice more afterward, most famously against George Foreman in Zaire in 1974, and was later diagnosed with Parkinson's syndrome.

Nefertiti's birth, around 1370 BCE, left no record of her parentage; she may have been Egyptian nobility or, by one theory, a Mitanni princess sent to seal an alliance. What is certain is that she married Akhenaten and appears beside him in more temple reliefs than any queen before her, driving a chariot and making offerings to the Aten in scenes usually reserved for kings.

The painted limestone bust that made her famous was found in 1912 in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose at Akhetaten, one plaster-coated practice piece among many, never intended for display. It sat in a German museum for over a decade before its 1924 unveiling turned an unfinished study into the most reproduced face of ancient Egypt.

Neil Armstrong was born in Wapakoneta, Ohio, in 1930 and earned his student pilot's licence on his sixteenth birthday, before he could legally drive. He flew 78 combat missions as a Navy pilot in Korea, including one in which his jet was struck by a wire strung across a valley, an incident he survived by ejecting over rice paddies.

Before Apollo, Armstrong commanded Gemini 8 in 1966, a mission that nearly killed him when a stuck thruster sent the docked spacecraft into a violent spin he had to fight to bring under control. He was a civilian test pilot as well as an astronaut, and NASA's own accounting credits him with keeping the Apollo 11 lunar module steady after he manually flew it past a boulder field to a safer landing spot with less than 30 seconds of fuel remaining.

Nero was born in 37 CE at Antium, to Agrippina the Younger, whose marriage to the emperor Claudius and relentless manoeuvring got her son adopted ahead of Claudius's own biological son Britannicus. Agrippina is widely suspected, though not proven, of poisoning Claudius in 54 CE to put fifteen-year-old Nero on the throne while she still controlled him.

He later had his own mother killed once she became inconvenient, and Roman writers, largely hostile senators writing after his fall, blamed him for singing while Rome burned in 64 CE and for using Christians as scapegoats for the fire, a detail Tacitus records independently of Nero's own later reputation for cruelty. He died by his own hand in 68 CE as army revolts closed in, ending the Julio-Claudian dynasty.

Isaac Newton was born prematurely in Woolsthorpe, small enough that he was not expected to survive the day. He later spent much of 1665 and 1666 back at his mother's farm after Cambridge closed because of plague, and it was in that stretch away from the university, not in a lecture hall, that he worked out much of his early thinking on calculus, optics and gravity.

The story of an apple falling on his head is almost certainly invented, though Newton himself told a version of it late in life in which he simply watched an apple fall in the orchard and started wondering why it fell straight down rather than sideways. The Principia, published in 1687, turned that question into laws that described the motion of everything from apples to planets with the same mathematics.

Bohr's 1913 model placed electrons in fixed orbits that could only jump between set energy levels, absorbing or releasing light in the process. It broke physics as much as it explained it: the idea worked, matched observed spectra, and had no basis in the classical mechanics everyone had trained on.

He later ran an institute in Copenhagen that became a meeting point for the physicists building quantum theory, arguing through what came to be called the Copenhagen interpretation. In 1943, warned that the Gestapo planned to arrest him, he escaped occupied Denmark by fishing boat to Sweden and went on to work at Los Alamos.

Friedrich Nietzsche was born on 15 October 1844 in Rocken, a village in Prussian Saxony, the son of a Lutheran pastor who died when Nietzsche was four. He grew up in a household of women, his mother, sister and grandmother, and was known as a devout, serious child before university study of classical philology pulled him toward philosophy instead.

He held a professorship at Basel in his twenties, an unusually early appointment, but chronic illness forced him to resign by 1879 and he spent the following decade writing while moving between boarding houses in Switzerland and Italy. Nearly all his major books sold poorly in his lifetime; Thus Spoke Zarathustra's fourth part was printed in only forty copies. He suffered a collapse in Turin in January 1889 and never wrote again, dying in 1900.

Nightingale is remembered for the lamp, but her real weapon was a chart. Arriving at the British military hospital at Scutari in 1854, she found more soldiers dying of typhus, cholera and dysentery from filthy wards than of wounds. She pushed for scrubbed floors, working sewers and clean linen, and afterwards used statistical diagrams, including a rose-shaped chart of her own design, to show Parliament exactly what had been killing men.

She was born in Florence in 1820, the city her wealthy English parents named her after. Back in London she founded a nursing school at St Thomas' Hospital in 1860, the first of its kind not run by a religious order, and spent much of the rest of her life bedridden yet still writing reports that reshaped hospital design across Britain.

Khrushchev started as a metal worker and rose through the Communist Party under Stalin, whose purges he helped carry out in Ukraine before becoming Soviet leader after Stalin's death in 1953. On 25 February 1956 he delivered a speech to a closed session of the Twentieth Party Congress, describing Stalin's mass arrests and executions and the false confessions extracted by torture.

The speech was meant to stay within the party, but copies circulated and it reached foreign intelligence services within months, shaking communist governments across Eastern Europe. Six years later he approved sending nuclear missiles to Cuba, provoking a standoff with the United States that came closer than any other Cold War episode to direct nuclear conflict.

Nikola Tesla was born on 10 July 1856 in Smiljan, a village in what is now Croatia then part of the Austrian Empire, the son of an Orthodox priest. He studied engineering in Graz and Prague without finishing a degree, then emigrated to the United States in 1884 to work briefly for Thomas Edison, whose company favoured direct current, the system Tesla's own designs were about to make obsolete.

After the two fell out over money, Tesla developed alternating current motors and transformers and sold the patents to George Westinghouse, whose company used them to light the 1893 Chicago World's Fair and to harness Niagara Falls for long-distance power transmission. He spent his later decades on speculative projects, including an unfinished wireless power tower on Long Island, and died in 1943 out of the public eye and in debt.

Orson Welles was born on 6 May 1915 in Kenosha, Wisconsin, and was staging his own theatre productions with borrowed money before he was out of his teens. In 1938 his radio adaptation of The War of the Worlds, staged as a series of fake news bulletins, reportedly unsettled listeners who tuned in partway and mistook it for a real invasion.

RKO gave him, at 24, a contract with almost total creative control over his first film, an arrangement no studio had offered a newcomer before. Citizen Kane, released in 1941, used deep-focus photography and a fractured, flashback structure to trace a newspaper tycoon modelled partly on William Randolph Hearst, who tried to have the film buried before it opened.

Orville Wright was born on 19 August 1871 in Dayton, Ohio, four years after his brother Wilbur, and the two ran a bicycle shop that gave them both the mechanical skill and the spare cash to chase powered flight as a side project rather than a funded programme. Neither brother went to university.

On the morning of 17 December 1903, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville made the first of the day's four flights, covering 120 feet in twelve seconds while Wilbur ran alongside the wing, and a bystander from a nearby lifesaving station snapped the one photograph that fixed the moment in history. Orville outlived Wilbur by more than three decades, dying in 1948 after seeing aviation transformed by jet engines.

Oscar Wilde was born on 16 October 1854 in Dublin to a surgeon father and a mother who wrote poetry and hosted a literary salon. He studied classics at Trinity College Dublin and then Oxford, where he won the Newdigate Prize for poetry and began cultivating the flamboyant public persona, velvet coats and epigrams, that made him famous in London before he had written any of the plays he is now known for.

The Importance of Being Earnest opened in February 1895 to acclaim, but within months Wilde was on trial, first as a plaintiff in a failed libel case against the Marquess of Queensberry, then as a defendant charged with gross indecency for relationships with men. He was convicted and sentenced to two years' hard labour, and left prison in 1897 broke and largely shunned, dying in Paris three years later.

Ovid was born in 43 BCE in Sulmo, east of Rome, to a family that expected him to pursue law and public office, a path he tried and abandoned in favour of poetry. His early work was frankly erotic, and it made him famous in Rome well before he turned to the mythological retellings that would outlast the scandal.

The Metamorphoses, completed around 8 CE, strings together some 250 myths of transformation into a single continuous narrative, from the creation of the world to Julius Caesar becoming a star. That same year Augustus exiled Ovid to a remote outpost on the Black Sea, for reasons never stated plainly in surviving sources, and he died there roughly a decade later, still writing but never recalled.

Neruda was born Ricardo Eliecer Neftali Reyes Basoalto in the Chilean town of Parral, and adopted his pen name as a teenager, partly to keep his writing hidden from a father who disapproved of poetry. Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair, published when he was twenty, sold widely across the Spanish-speaking world and was still in print decades later.

He was also a Chilean diplomat and senator, and was forced into hiding and exile in 1948 after the government he had once supported turned on the Communist Party he belonged to, crossing the Andes on horseback to escape arrest. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971 and died in 1973, days after the coup that overthrew President Salvador Allende, a friend of his; the exact cause of his death is still disputed.

Picasso was born in Malaga in 1881 and was drawing before he could reliably speak, according to family legend his first word was a demand for a pencil. His full baptismal name ran to over twenty words, honouring saints and relatives, and he later signed his work simply with his mother's surname.

Around 1907, alongside Georges Braque, he began breaking objects into overlapping planes seen from several angles at once, the style known as Cubism, which unsettled the assumption that a painting should show one fixed viewpoint. Guernica, painted in 1937 after the bombing of the Basque town during the Spanish Civil War, is a mural-sized canvas he refused to let hang in Spain while Franco ruled.

Blaise Pascal built his first calculating machine, the Pascaline, at eighteen to help his father total up tax accounts in Rouen. It could add and subtract using a set of geared dials, with carries handled mechanically, and Pascal produced roughly fifty of them over the following years, though the machines proved too costly for most buyers and never sold well.

He treated mathematics as one interest among several. A dispute over gambling odds, put to him by a friend, led him into a correspondence with Fermat that founded probability theory. Later in life he turned largely to religious writing, and the Pensees, published after his death in 1662, are fragments of an argument for Christian faith he never lived to finish.

Paul Cezanne was born on 19 January 1839 in Aix-en-Provence, the son of a hat maker turned banker who wanted him to study law. He trained as a lawyer for a time before his father relented and let him move to Paris to paint, though the family's money kept him afloat through decades in which almost nobody bought his work.

Cezanne exhibited with the Impressionists early on but pulled away from their loose brushwork, returning obsessively to the same motifs, Mont Sainte-Victoire, apples on a tablecloth, bathers by a riverbank, to work out how solid form could survive on a flat canvas. Both Matisse and Picasso later called him the father of modern painting, and the geometric planes he built out of colour patches fed directly into Cubism after his death in 1906.

Paul Revere was born in Boston in 1735 and worked as a silversmith, a trade that also made him a skilled engraver of political propaganda; his print of the Boston Massacre, more dramatic than accurate, helped turn colonial opinion against the British garrison.

His ride on the night of 18 April 1775 was one of several; he was joined by William Dawes and Samuel Prescott, and it was Prescott who actually reached Concord, since Revere was captured by a British patrol partway there. Longfellow's 1861 poem, written decades later to stir Union feeling, is what fixed Revere alone in the story.

Petrarch was born Francesco Petrarca in 1304 in Arezzo, where his father had been exiled from Florence in the same political purges that had exiled Dante. He trained in law at his father's insistence but abandoned it after his father died, choosing instead to hunt down and copy classical Latin manuscripts, a pursuit that helped revive texts Europe had largely lost track of.

His sonnets to a woman he called Laura, whom he said he first saw in an Avignon church in 1327, made vernacular Italian poetry a model for centuries of European love poetry. He was crowned poet laureate in Rome in 1341, a ceremony he had lobbied for himself, and his letters and essays did as much as his poems to shape what later generations called humanism.

Pierre Curie was born in Paris on 15 May 1859 and made his name in physics years before he met Marie: with his brother Jacques he discovered piezoelectricity, the electric charge certain crystals produce under mechanical stress, while still in his early twenties. He was already an established researcher when a mutual colleague introduced him to a Polish student named Marya Sklodowska in 1894.

Pierre set aside his own crystal research to work with her on the intensely radioactive ore pitchblende, and the couple isolated polonium and radium together within a single year. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Marie and Henri Becquerel, but died three years later, struck by a horse-drawn cart while crossing a Paris street in the rain.

Plato was born in Athens around 428 BCE to an aristocratic family with connections on both sides to earlier Athenian statesmen. He first trained for a political career, but the trial and execution of his teacher Socrates in 399 BCE, on charges of corrupting the young, turned him against Athenian democracy as it then operated and toward philosophy instead.

He founded the Academy around 387 BCE on land just outside Athens, an institution that ran for centuries after his death and is sometimes called the first university in the Western tradition. Nearly all his surviving work takes the form of dialogues rather than treatises, most of them starring Socrates, which leaves scholars still arguing over where the teacher's ideas end and the student's begin.

Almost nothing survives about Ptolemy's personal life beyond that he worked in Alexandria around 100 to 170 CE, using observational records kept there and in Babylon going back centuries before his own time. Even his first name and family background are unrecorded; he is known only by the name attached to his books.

His Almagest set out a mathematical model of a stationary Earth with the sun, moon and planets circling it on nested spheres, detailed enough to predict eclipses and planetary positions with real accuracy. That geocentric model went essentially unchallenged in both the Islamic and European scholarly worlds for roughly fourteen centuries, until Copernicus and later Kepler replaced it.

Pythagoras was born on the island of Samos around 570 BCE and later settled in Croton, in southern Italy, where he founded a community that mixed mathematics with strict dietary rules, secrecy oaths and a belief in the transmigration of souls. He wrote nothing down himself; everything attributed to him comes from followers writing after his death.

The theorem bearing his name was already known, in specific numerical cases, to Babylonian and Egyptian mathematicians centuries earlier. What the Pythagorean school likely contributed was a general proof and, more lastingly, the idea that number itself explained the structure of the physical world, an idea that outlasted every detail of his biography.

Rabindranath Tagore was born on 7 May 1861 in Calcutta into a wealthy, culturally prominent Bengali family, one of thirteen surviving children, and was largely educated at home after finding formal schooling stifling. He began writing poetry as a child and had published his first substantial collection by his teens.

In 1913 he became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, awarded for Gitanjali, a collection he had translated himself into English prose. He later renounced the British knighthood he had been given, in protest at the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre in Amritsar, and went on to found Visva-Bharati University as an experiment in education free of national boundaries.

Ralph Waldo Emerson was born in Boston on 25 May 1803 into a family of ministers, and trained for the pulpit himself before resigning his Unitarian church post in 1832 over doubts about the ritual of communion. He turned to lecturing and essay writing instead, a shift that let him keep preaching in everything but name.

His 1836 essay Nature laid out the ideas that became Transcendentalism, arguing that individuals could reach truth directly through intuition and the natural world rather than through inherited doctrine or institutions. He helped gather the circle of writers around Concord, Massachusetts, including Henry David Thoreau, who lived on land Emerson owned while writing Walden.

Ramesses was born around 1303 BCE to a father, Seti I, who was not himself born to rule. His grandfather Ramesses I had been a military commander elevated to found a new dynasty, so the boy was raised from early childhood as a designated heir, given military commands and his own household years before he took the throne around age twenty-five.

His reign, which ran some sixty-six years, is documented less by any single record than by sheer volume: temples at Abu Simbel and Karnak, a peace treaty with the Hittites preserved in both Egyptian and Akkadian copies, and a mummy so recognisable that when it flew to Paris in 1976 for fungal treatment, Egypt issued it a passport listing its occupation as king, deceased.

Raphael was born in Urbino in 1483, the son of a court painter who died when the boy was eleven, leaving him to complete his training in his father's workshop and then under Perugino. He arrived in Rome still in his mid twenties and within a few years was working directly for Pope Julius II, an unusually fast ascent for an artist without an established Roman reputation.

The School of Athens, painted for the papal apartments starting around 1509, gathers ancient philosophers into a single hall and gives several of their faces the features of Raphael's contemporaries, including Leonardo as Plato. Raphael died on his thirty seventh birthday in 1520, reportedly from a fever, having produced an enormous body of work in a working life that lasted barely two decades.

Rembrandt was born in Leiden, the son of a miller, and made his fortune in Amsterdam painting the city's merchants and civic guards before losing most of it to bad investments and an expensive house he could not afford. He was declared insolvent in 1656 and had to auction off his art collection and possessions.

The Night Watch, finished in 1642, is technically a group portrait of a militia company, though Rembrandt broke every convention of the genre by staging the men in mid-movement rather than lined up for a formal pose. Some of the guardsmen who paid for the painting reportedly complained they were too hard to pick out in the crowd, buried behind more prominent figures Rembrandt chose to light.

Pierre-Auguste Renoir was born on 25 February 1841 in Limoges, a city known for porcelain, and he began his working life painting decorative designs onto china before he could afford formal art training. That trade taught him to work fast and to think in flat areas of colour, both of which carried over when he started painting outdoors alongside Monet in the early 1860s.

Renoir's most crowded canvases, dance halls and riverside lunches thick with figures, took months of outdoor sittings to finish, an unusual commitment for work that reads as spontaneous. In the 1880s he broke with the loose brushwork of his Impressionist years and spent time studying Renaissance painting in Italy, returning to sharper outlines and more classical figures for the rest of his career.

Richard Feynman was born on 11 May 1918 in Queens, New York, and taught himself trigonometry and calculus from library books while still at school. During the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos, still in his twenties, he ran the group's calculations by hand and mechanical calculator and moonlighted by picking the combination locks on colleagues' safes for sport.

His 1965 Nobel Prize, shared with Julian Schwinger and Sin-Itiro Tomonaga, recognised a way of calculating how light and matter interact using simple diagrams now taught to every physics student.
