In 1986 he served on the panel investigating the Challenger disaster and demonstrated on live television, by squeezing a rubber O-ring seal in a glass of ice water, why the material had failed in the cold.

Richard was born in 1157 at Oxford, the third son of Henry II, which made his path to the English throne accidental rather than assured: two older brothers died before their father did. He grew up largely in Aquitaine, his mother Eleanor's inheritance, and spoke French rather than English, a language he may never have learned at all.

His reputation for military skill was built mostly outside England. He spent barely six months of his ten-year reign in the country he ruled, campaigning instead in the Holy Land and in France. Captured on his way home from the Third Crusade in 1192, he was held for ransom by the Holy Roman Emperor for over a year until England paid a sum equal to several years of royal income.

Richard Nixon was born on 9 January 1913 in a house his father built in Yorba Linda, California, above the family's citrus grove. He entered national politics as a young congressman on the House committee investigating Alger Hiss, then was Eisenhower's vice president before losing the 1960 presidential race to John F. Kennedy by one of the narrowest margins on record.

His 1972 visit to China ended more than two decades without diplomatic contact between the countries, arranged in secret by Henry Kissinger. Two years later, facing near-certain impeachment over the Watergate break-in and its cover-up, he became the only US president to resign, on 9 August 1974. His successor, Gerald Ford, pardoned him a month afterward.

Richard Strauss was born in Munich on 11 June 1864, the son of a court horn player whose conservative musical taste shaped his son's early training even as the young Strauss pushed toward the more radical harmony of Wagner and Liszt. By his twenties he was already a sought-after conductor as well as a composer.

His tone poems of the 1880s and 1890s, including Also sprach Zarathustra and Don Juan, made his reputation as an orchestral colourist before he turned to opera. Der Rosenkavalier, premiered in Dresden in 1911, became his most popular stage work, a comedy of manners set in eighteenth-century Vienna that contrasted sharply with the violent modernism of his earlier opera Salome.

Richard Wagner was born in Leipzig on 22 May 1813, and his early career was less music than debt and flight: he worked as a jobbing conductor across several German and Baltic towns, ran up bills he could not pay, and at one point fled Riga at night to escape creditors before eventually taking refuge in political exile after joining an uprising in Dresden in 1849.

He built the Ring cycle around leitmotifs, short musical phrases tied to a character or idea that recur and combine across four full operas lasting around fifteen hours in total. To stage it properly he had a purpose-built theatre constructed at Bayreuth, funded partly by King Ludwig II of Bavaria, who idolised him and covered his debts more than once. His antisemitic writings later made him one of the most contested figures in music history.

Robert Bruce was born in 1274 into a family with its own claim to the Scottish crown, a claim that put him on both sides of the independence struggle before he settled on one. He briefly submitted to Edward I of England and fought alongside him, then broke away and had himself crowned king of Scots in 1306, months after killing a rival claimant in a church.

Excommunicated for that killing and hunted as a fugitive for years, he rebuilt his position through a guerrilla campaign that avoided open battle until his army was strong enough to risk one. At Bannockburn in June 1314 his forces defeated a much larger English relief army trying to reach besieged Stirling Castle, a victory that did not end the war but forced England to eventually recognise Scottish independence in 1328.

Robert Burns was born in 1759 to a tenant farmer in Ayrshire and spent much of his short life doing hard physical farm work between writing poems in Scots dialect, a language the educated Edinburgh literary world had mostly abandoned for English.

His 1786 collection made him famous almost overnight, and he later collected and reworked older folk songs rather than claiming pure originality, which is how Auld Lang Syne reached him. He died in 1796 at thirty-seven, and Burns Night suppers, held on his birthday every 25 January, are older than almost any other writer's commemorated anniversary.

Oppenheimer was chosen to run the Manhattan Project's Los Alamos laboratory despite having no Nobel Prize, no experience managing a large team, and a security file flagged for past ties to leftist politics. General Leslie Groves picked him anyway, betting on a scientific breadth that let Oppenheimer talk across the whole project rather than only his own specialty.

After the Trinity test in July 1945, Oppenheimer later said he thought of a line from the Bhagavad Gita, though the exact wording and when he first recited it are disputed even by people who knew him. His postwar opposition to the hydrogen bomb led a 1954 security hearing to strip his clearance, a decision the United States government formally vacated in 2022, sixty-eight years later.

Rosa Parks was born Rosa Louise McCauley on 4 February 1913 in Tuskegee, Alabama, and was already an active secretary of the local NAACP chapter years before her arrest, not the tired seamstress of later legend. On 1 December 1955 she refused a Montgomery bus driver's order to give up her seat to a white passenger, and was arrested for violating the city's segregation ordinance.

The arrest triggered a boycott organised largely by local Black churches and a young pastor named Martin Luther King Jr., who was chosen partly because he was new to town and had few enemies yet. The boycott lasted 381 days and ended only after the Supreme Court struck down Montgomery's bus segregation law. Parks lost her department store job over the case and later moved to Detroit.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau's mother died days after his birth in Geneva, and he was raised largely by his father until the man fled the city over a legal dispute, leaving Rousseau in the care of relatives. He worked as an engraver's apprentice, a footman and a music copyist before his writing found an audience in his late thirties.

The Social Contract, published in 1762, opened with the line that man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains, arguing that legitimate political authority comes only from the general will of the people governed. The book was banned and burned in Geneva and Paris within weeks of publication, and Rousseau spent much of the rest of his life moving between countries to avoid arrest.

Peter Paul Rubens ran his Antwerp studio like a factory, dozens of assistants turning out altarpieces for churches across Catholic Europe, and still found time to work as a spy. From 1628 he carried secret correspondence between the Spanish crown and its agents, and in 1629 Philip IV sent him to London to help negotiate an end to a war between Spain and England that had run for the better part of two decades.

The treaty was signed in Madrid in November 1630, and both Charles I and Philip IV knighted him for his part in it. Cambridge gave him an honorary degree the same year. He kept painting throughout, turning his diplomatic travels into portrait commissions from the courts he was supposed to be quietly working on, a double career few other painters ever managed.

Rudyard Kipling was born in Bombay on 30 December 1865, and named after the English lake where his parents had courted, though he spent much of his childhood in England, separated from his family for years in a foster arrangement he later described as bleak. He returned to India as a teenager to work as a journalist, the job that gave him the material for his early stories.

In 1907 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature at forty-one, still the youngest recipient and the first writing in English, largely for verse and stories like The Jungle Book that drew on his Indian years. His later reputation suffered over his defence of empire, but he turned down both a knighthood and the post of Poet Laureate, preferring to remain simply a writer.

Saladin, born Yusuf ibn Ayyub in 1137 in Tikrit, came from a Kurdish family serving Muslim rulers in Iraq and Syria. He rose through his uncle's military household in Egypt rather than through any dynastic claim, and only became sultan after the Fatimid caliphate he had served collapsed and he took its place in 1171.

Uniting Egypt and Syria took him more than a decade of campaigning against rival Muslim emirs before he ever faced the Crusader kingdoms directly. His decisive victory came at the Battle of Hattin in 1187, which broke the Crusader field army and let him retake Jerusalem within months. He treated the city's Christian population with notable leniency, ransoming rather than massacring most of the surrendered garrison.

Dali was born nine months after an older brother, also named Salvador, had died as a toddler, and his parents told him he was that brother's reincarnation. He later said the belief shaped his lifelong obsession with doubles, mirrors and his own identity, themes that run through much of his painting.

The Persistence of Memory, his 1931 canvas of limp watches draped over a barren landscape, is smaller than most people expect from reproductions, roughly the size of a sheet of paper. Dali claimed the melting clocks came from watching a wheel of Camembert cheese soften in the sun. He was expelled from Spain's Surrealist circle in 1934 for his ambivalence toward fascism and continued painting into his eighties despite Parkinson's disease.

Samuel Morse was born in Charlestown, Massachusetts, on 27 April 1791 and trained as a painter, not an engineer; he made his living for years off portraits and history paintings, including a large group portrait of the U.S. House of Representatives. The turn towards telegraphy came only after his wife died in 1825 while he was away painting a commission, and the news reached him days too late for him to say goodbye.

He patented an electric telegraph in the 1830s and, with Alfred Vail, worked out the system of dots and dashes that let a single wire carry language. In 1844 he sent the message What hath God wrought from Washington to Baltimore over the first long-distance line, funded by Congress after years of lobbying. He spent much of his later life defending his sole claim to the invention against rival inventors.

Sappho was born on Lesbos around 630 BCE into a family wealthy enough that her exile at one point, ordered for unclear political reasons, took her to Sicily rather than anywhere harsher. Almost none of this comes from Sappho herself; it is pieced together from later biographers writing centuries after she died.

Of the roughly nine books of verse ancient scholars attributed to her, only one poem survives complete, quoted whole by a later critic illustrating a point about style. The rest exists as fragments, some recovered from papyrus used to stuff mummified crocodiles in Roman Egypt, scraps that still shape how the word lyric is understood.

Arthur Schopenhauer was born in Danzig on 22 February 1788 into a merchant family that expected him to take over the firm, and he spent years training as a businessman before persuading his mother to let him study philosophy instead. She never forgave him for it; the two eventually stopped speaking altogether.

His major work, The World as Will and Representation, appeared in 1818 and sold almost nothing, remaindered within a few years. He kept revising it anyway, largely ignored by German academic philosophy for decades while Hegel drew the crowds. Recognition arrived only late in his life, once a wider readership, including a young Friedrich Nietzsche, found value in his bleak account of human striving.

Seneca was born around 4 BCE in Corduba, in Roman Spain, to a wealthy family of Roman citizens, and was sent to Rome as a child for the education expected of a future senator. He built a career as advocate, essayist and playwright before Emperor Claudius exiled him to Corsica in 41 CE on charges linked to a court affair.

Recalled to tutor the young Nero, he became the emperor's chief adviser for the early, relatively stable years of the reign, then watched that same emperor turn on him. Nero eventually forced Seneca to take his own life in 65 CE on suspicion of conspiracy, a death Tacitus describes at length as calm and deliberately staged to match the Stoic philosophy Seneca had spent his career writing about.

Prokofiev left Soviet Russia in 1918, toured Europe and the United States as a pianist and composer for nearly two decades, then chose in 1936 to move back to a country now run by Stalin. Few Western artists made that trade in reverse, and the reasons he gave friends, homesickness and a wish to write for Soviet audiences, never fully explained the risk.

He wrote Peter and the Wolf that same year for a Moscow children's theatre, assigning each character its own instrument so young audiences could learn to pick out an orchestra's parts by ear. Official Soviet criticism of his music followed him for the rest of his life; he died on 5 March 1953, the same day as Stalin, and his death was barely reported for days because the state's attention was elsewhere.

Rachmaninoff was born in 1873 on a country estate in Russia that his family soon lost to debt. The failure of his First Symphony in 1897, savaged by critics and possibly conducted drunk by Alexander Glazunov, left him unable to compose for roughly three years, a depression he later said was lifted through hypnotherapy sessions with a doctor named Nikolai Dahl.

The result, his Second Piano Concerto of 1901, became one of the most performed works in the repertoire and he dedicated it to Dahl in gratitude. He left Russia for good after the 1917 revolution, settling eventually in the United States, where he supported himself largely through concert touring as a pianist rather than through the composing he had once feared he had lost.

Sigmund Freud was born on 6 May 1856 in Freiberg, Moravia, then part of the Austrian Empire and now Pribor in the Czech Republic, the eldest of eight children in a Jewish wool-merchant's family that moved to Vienna when he was four. He trained as a neurologist and spent years researching cocaine's medical uses and the physiology of the nervous system before turning to the theory of the mind he is remembered for.

Working with hysteria patients in the 1890s, Freud developed the idea that symptoms could stem from repressed memories, accessible through free association and dream interpretation. The Interpretation of Dreams, published in 1899 though dated 1900, sold only a few hundred copies at first. Freud fled Vienna for London in 1938 after the Nazi annexation of Austria, and died there the following year.

Simon Bolivar was born in Caracas in 1783 into a wealthy Creole family, orphaned young, and educated partly through the Enlightenment texts his tutor gave him, ideas that later shaped his politics far more than the family's mining fortune did.

Between 1813 and 1824 his armies fought Spanish forces across what are now Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia, the country later named for him. He tried to hold the liberated territories together as Gran Colombia, but rivalries among his own generals broke it apart within years of independence, and he died in 1830 believing the project had failed.

Beauvoir passed the demanding agregation exam in philosophy at twenty-one, the youngest person ever to do so at the time, finishing just behind Jean-Paul Sartre, with whom she began a lifelong intellectual partnership and open relationship that never involved marriage or living together.

The Second Sex, published in 1949, opened by asking what a woman actually is once biology is separated from the roles society assigns her, and its central claim, that one becomes a woman rather than being born one, gave later feminist theory a working vocabulary. The book was placed on the Vatican's list of forbidden reading and sold out its first printing within a week in France.

Isabella Baumfree was born enslaved in Swartekill, New York, around 1797, and was sold away from her family more than once before escaping to freedom in 1826 with her infant daughter. She later sued to recover a son who had been illegally sold south, and won, one of the first such cases brought by a Black woman against a white man in a United States court.

She took the name Sojourner Truth in 1843 after becoming a travelling preacher, and her 1851 address to a women's rights convention in Akron, Ohio, is now remembered chiefly through the line Ain't I a woman. That phrasing comes from an account published twelve years later by a white abolitionist; the contemporary newspaper transcript printed the same week does not contain it.

Solon was born in Athens around 630 BCE to a family of modest noble standing; ancient biographers say he took up trade as a young man partly because his father had given away much of the family's wealth. That mercantile background, unusual for an Athenian lawgiver, put him in contact with ordinary debtors and creditors before he ever held office.

Appointed archon around 594 BCE amid a crisis of debt bondage, he cancelled outstanding debts secured on people's bodies, opened political offices beyond the old aristocracy, and then, according to Plutarch, left Athens for ten years so nobody could pressure him into amending the laws himself.

Sophocles was born around 497 BCE in Colonus, near Athens, to a family wealthy enough from arms manufacturing that he received a full education in music and athletics before ever writing a play. He first defeated the established Aeschylus in the Athenian dramatic competition in 468 BCE, a result ancient sources say the judges reached only after the city's leading general was drafted in to break a tie.

He is credited with introducing a third actor into tragedy, which let him build scenes of direct confrontation, such as Antigone's clash with Creon, that two speakers could not sustain. Of some 120 plays attributed to him, only seven survive whole, and he was reportedly an Athenian general and a treasury official alongside a writing career that outlasted several wars.

Stephen Hawking was born in Oxford in 1942 and was diagnosed with motor neurone disease at 21, while a doctoral student at Cambridge, and given a prognosis of a few years to live. He lived with the disease for more than fifty years instead, losing the ability to speak unaided after a tracheotomy in 1985 and communicating from then on through a speech-generating device controlled by a single cheek muscle.

His technical work on singularities and black hole radiation, the process now called Hawking radiation, established that black holes are not entirely black but slowly emit energy and can in principle evaporate. A Brief History of Time, published in 1988, was written for a general audience, and it stayed on bestseller lists for years despite, by his own account, most buyers never finishing it.

Sun Tzu is traditionally placed in the sixth century BCE as a general serving the state of Wu, but the text bearing his name, The Art of War, contains passages some scholars date to the later Warring States period, generations after he supposedly lived. Whether one general wrote it or it accumulated over time is unresolved.

A 1972 excavation at Yinqueshan uncovered bamboo strips confirming the text existed by the second century BCE, along with a related but distinct work attributed to a descendant, Sun Bin. The find settled the book's antiquity without settling anything about the man; its advice to win without fighting has been read by strategists from feudal Japan to modern business schools.

Anthony voted illegally in the 1872 presidential election, registering and casting a ballot in Rochester, New York, to force the courts to rule on whether the Fourteenth Amendment already granted women that right. She was arrested, tried and fined 100 dollars, which she refused to pay, and the judge, wary of a Supreme Court appeal, declined to jail her over it.

Born in Massachusetts in 1820 to a Quaker family active in abolition, she partnered with Elizabeth Cady Stanton for decades on the suffrage campaign, editing a newspaper called The Revolution and touring the country lecturing. She died in 1906, fourteen years before the Nineteenth Amendment, which gave American women the vote, was ratified.

Tamerlane was born in 1336 near Samarkand, in a Turkicised Mongol clan with no claim to Genghisid royal blood, which is why he ruled as an emir rather than a khan throughout his life, marrying into the Genghis line instead to borrow its legitimacy. An injury early in his career, probably from an arrow, left him lame in one leg, the likely source of the nickname Timur-e Lang, Timur the Lame.

His campaigns from the 1370s onward reached from Delhi to Moscow to Damascus, and were marked by mass killing used deliberately as a psychological weapon: towers of skulls left outside cities that had resisted were meant to make the next city surrender without a fight. He died in 1405 marching to invade Ming China, and the empire he built fractured among his descendants within decades.

Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was born on 7 May 1840 in Votkinsk, a Russian industrial town where his father ran a metalworks. He trained first for a career in the civil service, working as a clerk in the justice ministry, before enrolling at the newly founded Saint Petersburg Conservatory in his early twenties and turning to music full time.

He supported himself for years through a strange arrangement with a wealthy widow, Nadezhda von Meck, who funded him generously on the condition that they never meet in person, corresponding instead by letter for over a decade. Swan Lake was received coolly at its 1877 premiere and only became a staple after his death, when a revised staging in Saint Petersburg in 1895 fixed the choreography still used today.

Theodore Roosevelt was born on 27 October 1858 in a brownstone on Manhattan's East 20th Street, a sickly asthmatic child who built his own body through what he called the strenuous life: boxing, hiking and weightlifting became a lifelong habit rather than a phase. He entered politics through the unglamorous route of the New York State Assembly at twenty-three.

He became president at forty-two, the youngest to hold the office, after William McKinley's assassination in 1901, having spent barely six months as vice president. In office he pursued antitrust suits against corporate trusts, pushed conservation policy that set aside roughly 230 million acres of public land, and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1906 for mediating the end of the Russo-Japanese War.

Thomas was born around 1225 near Aquino, south of Rome, into a noble family that expected him to become a Benedictine abbot, a position with real income attached. He joined the Dominicans instead, a newer order of mendicant friars living on alms, a choice his family opposed strongly enough that they reportedly held him captive for close to a year to try to change his mind.

He studied under Albert the Great in Paris and Cologne before teaching himself, at a time when Aristotle's works were still viewed with suspicion by much of the Church. The Summa Theologica, left unfinished at his death in 1274, was structured as a teaching text, question after question weighing objections against each other, and it became the standard reference for Catholic theology only well after he died.

Thomas Edison was born on 11 February 1847 in Milan, Ohio, and was largely taught at home after a teacher called him slow. Partial deafness set in during childhood, which he later said helped him concentrate by shutting out distraction. He worked as a telegraph operator in his teens, learning the industry from the inside before turning to invention full time.

In 1876 he built a dedicated research facility at Menlo Park, New Jersey, staffed with machinists and chemists working on multiple projects at once, a structure historians treat as the first industrial research lab rather than a lone inventor's workshop. It produced the phonograph in 1877 and a workable incandescent light bulb by 1879, along with a patent count that reached over a thousand by the time of his death in 1931.

Thomas Hardy was born on 2 June 1840 in Higher Bockhampton, Dorset, and trained first as an architect, working on church restorations before he could afford to write full time. Wessex, the setting for his novels, was his own invention, a fictionalised version of the counties of southwest England stitched together from real market towns and villages he renamed.

Critical fury over Tess of the d'Urbervilles and Jude the Obscure, both accused of indecency for their treatment of sex and religion, pushed Hardy away from fiction altogether after 1895. He spent his last three decades writing poetry instead, producing roughly a thousand poems, and asked that his epitaph carry no mention of the novels that had made him famous.

Thomas Hobbes claimed his mother went into labour early because of the fear sweeping England in April 1588, with the Spanish Armada rumoured to be approaching. He liked to say fear was his twin, born alongside him. Whether or not the story is exact, he spent much of his adult life circling the same subject: what people will accept to avoid being afraid of each other.

Leviathan, published in 1651 after years of civil war had shown him what a collapsed state looked like, argued that people surrender their freedoms to a sovereign in exchange for protection from a life he described as nasty, brutish and short. The book's frontispiece shows a giant crowned figure made up of hundreds of tiny citizens, a single image doing the work of the whole argument.

Thomas Jefferson was born in 1743 in Virginia and trained as a lawyer, and at thirty-three he was handed the drafting of the Declaration of Independence largely because his fellow committee members, Franklin and Adams among them, thought he wrote better prose than they did.

As president he sent Lewis and Clark west and, in 1803, bought the Louisiana Territory from France for roughly fifteen million dollars, doubling the country's size at about four cents an acre. He also enslaved over six hundred people across his lifetime, including Sally Hemings, with whom he fathered several children, a fact his own family long denied and DNA testing later confirmed.

Mann was born in Lubeck in 1875 into a family of grain merchants, and his first novel, Buddenbrooks, published when he was just twenty-five, traced the decline of a merchant family closely modelled on his own. It became a bestseller and, decades later, the work the Nobel committee cited by name when he won the Literature prize in 1929.

He wrote The Magic Mountain after a stay at a Swiss sanatorium visiting his wife, stretching what began as a novella into a sprawling meditation on illness and European civilisation before the First World War. A vocal critic of Nazism, he left Germany in 1933 and never returned to live there, eventually settling in the United States before spending his last years in Switzerland.

Thucydides was born in Athens around 460 BCE to a family with property near Thrace, wealth that let him serve as an elected general in the Peloponnesian War before the war itself derailed his career. In 424 BCE he was blamed for the loss of Amphipolis to a Spartan force and exiled from Athens, a punishment that gave him two decades to write rather than fight.

His history of that war deliberately excludes the gods as causes, sources speeches through reconstruction rather than invention, and states outright that he checked competing eyewitness accounts against each other. The method, more than any single fact he recorded, is why historians still cite him as the discipline's first methodological break from Herodotus.

Titian was born in the Alpine town of Pieve di Cadore, probably in 1488, though like several artists of his generation no baptismal record survives and later scholars have argued for dates as much as a decade apart. He was sent to Venice as a boy to train in the workshop of Giovanni Bellini, then the city's leading painter.

By his thirties he was working for the Venetian state and, later, for the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V and King Philip II of Spain, an international clientele few Italian painters of the period matched. His handling of colour, built up in layers rather than fixed by sharp outline, became the standard against which later Venetian painting was measured, and he kept painting into his eighties, well past when most contemporaries had died.

Trajan was born in 53 CE in Italica, in southern Spain, one of the first Roman emperors to come from a family settled outside Italy itself. He rose through a conventional military career under the Flavian emperors before Nerva, needing to shore up support from the army, adopted him as heir and successor in 97 CE.

Under Trajan the empire reached its largest territorial extent, following conquests in Dacia and a campaign against Parthia in the east. He also funded large public building programmes, including a new forum and market complex in Rome and a harbour at Ostia, projects the Senate later cited when granting him the honorific title optimus princeps, the best ruler.

Eliot was born in St Louis, Missouri, and did not settle in England until 1914, at 25. He became a British citizen in 1927, the same year he was confirmed into the Church of England, and later described himself, only half joking, as classicist, royalist, and Anglo-Catholic.

The Waste Land, published in 1922, ran to 434 lines stitched from fragments of Sanskrit, Dante, nursery rhyme, and pub conversation, and it arrived with his own footnotes because he suspected readers would need them. Ezra Pound cut the draft nearly in half; Eliot dedicated the finished poem to him as 'il miglior fabbro,' the better craftsman.

Tycho Brahe was born in 1546 into Danish nobility and was, by his own later account, effectively kidnapped as an infant by a wealthy childless uncle who raised him in place of his birth parents. He studied law at university but became fixated on astronomy after witnessing a solar eclipse that had been predicted in advance, a feat that struck him as close to magic.

A 1572 supernova he observed and carefully measured proved that the heavens were not, as ancient theory held, unchanging, and it made his reputation. King Frederick II funded him an entire island observatory, Uraniborg, where Brahe compiled the most precise naked-eye astronomical data yet recorded, later data his assistant Johannes Kepler used to derive the laws of planetary motion after Brahe's own death.

Vasco da Gama was born around 1460 in Sines, a small fortified port on the Alentejo coast, where his father commanded the town's garrison. No record fixes the exact date, and even the year is an estimate drawn from later documents rather than a birth register. He grew up in a minor noble household with ties to the sea, not the grand court connections that later biographies sometimes assume.

What made his 1497 voyage possible was not personal wealth but royal patronage: King Manuel I needed a commander who could hold a fleet together on a two-year journey with no reliable charts past the Cape of Good Hope. Da Gama was chosen over more senior captains, reached Calicut in 1498, and returned having lost more than half his crew, mostly to scurvy, a cost the crown judged worth the trade route it opened.

Diego Velazquez spent nearly four decades as court painter to Philip IV of Spain, close enough to the king that Philip is said to have given him a key to his private studio. His late masterpiece, Las Meninas, painted around 1656, shows the young Infanta Margarita surrounded by her attendants, with the artist himself visible at the edge working on a canvas the viewer cannot see.

A mirror at the back of the room reflects the king and queen, who appear to be standing where the viewer stands, watching the whole scene being painted. Art historians have argued for centuries about exactly what Velazquez was depicting, whether it is a portrait of the royal couple, a self-portrait, or a demonstration of painting itself, and the ambiguity has never really been resolved.

Victor Hugo was born in Besancon on 26 February 1802, the son of a Napoleonic general, and was already a published poet in his teens, winning a prize from the Academie Francaise before he was twenty. His 1830 play Hernani caused riots in the theatre between traditionalists and supporters of the new Romantic style, a fight remembered as the moment French drama broke from classical rules.

He spent nearly twenty years in exile on the Channel Islands after publicly opposing Napoleon III's seizure of power in 1851, and it was there, on Guernsey, that he finished Les Miserables in 1862. He returned to France a national figure and was given a state funeral in 1885 that drew roughly two million people onto the streets of Paris, one of the largest public gatherings the city had seen.

Vincent van Gogh was born on 30 March 1853 in Groot-Zundert, in the southern Netherlands, the son of a pastor, and he worked first as an art dealer and then briefly as a lay preacher among coal miners before turning to painting in his late twenties. He was almost entirely self-taught and sold only a handful of works while alive, kept afloat financially by his brother Theo, an art dealer in Paris.

He painted The Starry Night in June 1889 from memory, looking out the barred window of the asylum at Saint-Remy-de-Provence where he had committed himself after a breakdown. In just over a decade of painting he produced more than 2,000 works, most of them in the last two years of his life, before he died in July 1890 from a gunshot wound generally treated as self-inflicted.

Virgil was born near Mantua in 70 BCE to a family of modest landowning stock, and his early poetry, the Eclogues and Georgics, dealt with farming and rural life partly because his own family's land had been threatened by confiscations during the civil wars that followed Julius Caesar's assassination.

He spent the last decade of his life writing the Aeneid at the emperor Augustus's encouragement, tracing Rome's founding back to a Trojan refugee, and died in 19 BCE before finishing it to his own satisfaction. He reportedly asked for the manuscript to be burned unpublished; Augustus overruled him, and the unfinished epic became the standard school text of the Roman world instead.

Woolf was born in London in 1882 into a literary household, the daughter of a biographer and editor, and educated largely at home while her brothers went to Cambridge, a gap she resented and later wrote about directly in A Room of One's Own. After her father's death she and her siblings settled in Bloomsbury, giving their name to the circle of writers and artists who gathered there.

Novels such as Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse, both from the 1920s, compressed entire lives into a single day or a handful of scenes, moving fluidly between characters' inner thoughts rather than following a conventional plot. She suffered recurring bouts of severe depression throughout her life and drowned herself in the River Ouse in 1941, leaving a note to her husband taking care to say the illness, not him, was to blame.

Voltaire was born Francois-Marie Arouet and adopted the pen name as a young man, possibly an anagram built from a Latinised version of his surname. He was imprisoned in the Bastille twice before he turned thirty, once for writing verse insulting to the regent, and spent much of his adult life moving between courts and countries to stay ahead of censors he had angered.

Candide, published in 1759, mocked the fashionable idea that this is the best of all possible worlds by dragging its hero through earthquakes, executions and slavery. Voltaire wrote it while living at his own estate near the Swiss border, close enough to slip across if French authorities came looking, a precaution that turned out to be entirely characteristic of how he ran his career.

Disney was not the artist behind Mickey Mouse's final look. His collaborator Ub Iwerks drew the character that appeared in Steamboat Willie in 1928, refining Disney's rougher sketches into the round-eared figure audiences recognised. Disney provided Mickey's voice for two decades and was the one who understood, before most studios did, that synchronized sound was worth the risk.

His first feature, Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs in 1937, was widely predicted to fail. Hollywood insiders called it Disney's Folly, certain no audience would sit through eighty minutes of cartoon. It became the highest grossing film of its year and funded the studio that later built Disneyland, which opened in Anaheim in 1955 after Disney mortgaged his own life insurance policy to help pay for it.

Whitman set some of the type for the first edition of Leaves of Grass himself, in 1855, because he had worked as a printer and could not find a publisher willing to take it. He paid for the printing out of his own pocket and put no author's name on the spine, only an engraving of himself in a workman's shirt.

He was born on Long Island in 1819 and spent the Civil War years volunteering in Washington hospitals, dressing wounds and writing letters for soldiers who could not write themselves. He kept revising Leaves of Grass for the rest of his life, publishing new editions until the year he died, in 1892, so no two printings of the book are quite the same.

Walter Raleigh was born around 1552 in Devon to a gentry family without great wealth, and rose at Elizabeth I's court through a mix of military service, wit, and a widely repeated but unverified story that he laid his cloak over a puddle for the queen to walk on. He became one of her most favoured, and most resented, courtiers.

He financed the ill-fated Roanoke colony in the 1580s, an English settlement in what is now North Carolina that vanished without explanation sometime after 1587. His fortunes collapsed under James I, who imprisoned him in the Tower for over a decade and eventually had him executed in 1618 on a treason charge tied to an earlier conviction that had never been formally overturned.

Wassily Kandinsky was born in Moscow on 16 December 1866 and trained first in law and economics, only turning to painting seriously in his thirties after moving to Munich in 1896. He described a formative moment seeing one of his own paintings propped on its side, unrecognisable as a landscape, and finding it more powerful as pure shape and colour than it had been as a picture.

Around 1910 he began producing works with no recognisable subject at all, among the earliest fully abstract paintings in Western art, and he set out his reasoning in the book Concerning the Spiritual in Art. He later taught at the Bauhaus in Germany until the Nazi government closed the school in 1933, after which he settled in France for the rest of his life.

William Butler Yeats was born in Dublin on 13 June 1865, the son of a painter, and grew up dividing his time between Dublin, London and County Sligo, whose landscapes and folklore ran through his poetry for the rest of his life. He co-founded the Abbey Theatre in 1904 to give Irish writers a stage of their own, and was its director for decades.

Yeats won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923, cited for verse that gave expression to the spirit of an entire nation, shortly after Irish independence. He also sat as a senator in the new Irish Free State, and continued revising and publishing poetry into his seventies, producing some of his most admired work, including The Second Coming, in the last two decades of his life.

Heisenberg worked out matrix mechanics in 1925 while recovering from severe hay fever on the treeless island of Helgoland, staying awake through the night doing the arithmetic by hand. He was twenty-three, had no formal training in the matrix algebra his own equations required, and had to ask a colleague back in Gottingen to check that the mathematics even made sense.

During the Second World War he led Germany's nuclear research programme, which never came close to building a working reactor, let alone a bomb. Historians still argue why: whether he misjudged the physics, deliberately slowed the effort, or simply lacked the resources the Allies poured into the Manhattan Project. A secretly recorded 1945 conversation among captured German scientists is one of the few direct clues to what he believed.

Wilbur Wright was born on 16 April 1867 near Millville, Indiana, four years before his brother Orville, and the two ran a bicycle repair and manufacturing shop in Dayton, Ohio, that funded their early experiments with flight. Neither brother had a university degree; they taught themselves aerodynamics by building and testing their own wind tunnel.

The brothers chose the isolated dunes of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, for their trials because of its steady winds and soft sand for landings, and on 17 December 1903 Wilbur made the day's longest flight, 852 feet in fifty-nine seconds, after Orville's shorter first attempt. Wilbur died of typhoid fever in 1912, before commercial aviation had properly begun.

Wilhelm Rontgen was born on 27 March 1845 in Lennep, in what is now western Germany, and was expelled from technical school as a teenager for refusing to name a classmate who had drawn an unflattering caricature of a teacher. He had to sit an entrance exam in Switzerland instead, and built a career in experimental physics across several German universities before settling at Wurzburg.

In November 1895 he noticed a screen glowing in his darkened lab though it was shielded from the tube's visible light, and traced it to a form of radiation he could not identify, calling it X-radiation. He took an X-ray of his wife's hand, wedding ring visible through the bone, and published within weeks. In 1901 he won the first Nobel Prize in Physics and refused to patent the discovery, giving away the prize money.

William was born around 1028 in Falaise, in Normandy, the illegitimate son of Duke Robert I and a tanner's daughter named Herleva. Contemporaries called him William the Bastard long before Hastings gave him a better title. He became duke at about seven, when his father died on pilgrimage, and spent his minority surviving a string of assassination attempts by rival Norman nobles.

His claim to England rested on a disputed promise from Edward the Confessor and, he said, an oath sworn to him by Harold Godwinson himself. After landing near Hastings in September 1066, William won the battle in a single day when Harold was killed, then spent five more years crushing English revolts with a campaign of castle-building and land seizure that replaced most of the old aristocracy with Norman lords.

William Wordsworth was born in the Lake District in 1770 and was orphaned of both parents by thirteen, raised afterward by relatives and shaped, by his own account, by the fells and lakes around Cockermouth and Hawkshead that he wandered as a boy.

In 1798 he and Samuel Taylor Coleridge published Lyrical Ballads anonymously, using plain, ordinary language instead of the formal poetic diction readers expected, a choice that is often dated as the start of English Romanticism. He kept revising his long autobiographical poem, later titled The Prelude, for decades, and it was published only after his death in 1850.

Churchill was born prematurely at Blenheim Palace in 1874, two months ahead of schedule, during a dance his mother had attended the same evening. He struggled at school, failed the entrance exam to Sandhurst twice, and spent his twenties chasing action as a soldier and war correspondent, including a much publicised escape from a Boer prisoner of war camp in 1899.

By 1940, when he became prime minister, his career already included a disastrous term as First Lord of the Admiralty over the Gallipoli campaign and years out of government dismissed as a warmonger for his warnings about Germany. He wrote much of his own material, and the speeches he gave that year, refusing to negotiate as France fell, remain the reason he is remembered above the rest of his long and uneven career.

Wyatt Earp was born on 19 March 1848 in Monmouth, Illinois, and before he was any kind of lawman he worked as a buffalo hunter, a stagecoach guard and, by his own later admission, a horse thief who briefly jumped bail in Arkansas. He drifted through boomtowns across the Midwest and Southwest doing whatever paid, gambling included, long before Tombstone made him famous.

The gunfight associated with his name took place on 26 October 1881, not actually inside the corral itself but in a narrow lot beside it, in a roughly thirty-second exchange between the Earp brothers and Doc Holliday on one side and a loose group of cattle rustlers on the other. Three men died. The shootout grew far more famous decades later through films and television than it was at the time, one violent incident among many in a mining town.

Yuri Gagarin was born in 1934 in Klushino, a village his family was forced from when a German officer occupied their home during the war, leaving them in a mud hut for nearly two years. He trained as a foundryman and studied at a technical school before joining a flying club, and was selected for the Soviet cosmonaut corps in 1960 from more than 200 candidates partly for his short stature, which suited the cramped Vostok capsule.

His flight on 12 April 1961 lasted 108 minutes and made one orbit of the Earth; he did not pilot the descent, since the capsule was controlled from the ground, and he ejected and parachuted down separately near the landing site. He became a global celebrity afterward and died in 1968 in a jet training accident whose cause remains disputed.

Alexander Hamilton and Aaron Burr, the sitting vice president, met on the New Jersey cliffs above Weehawken on 11 July 1804 after years of political rivalry curdled into personal insult during a bitter New York governor's race. Duelling was already illegal in New York, which is exactly why both men rowed across the Hudson to fight it in New Jersey instead.

Accounts differ on what happened in the seconds after the signal: Hamilton's own second insisted he fired into the air on purpose, having decided beforehand that duelling was wrong, while Burr's second claimed Hamilton aimed and missed. What is agreed is that Burr's shot did not miss. It struck Hamilton above the hip and lodged near his spine, and he died in New York the following afternoon, at forty seven.

Antoine Lavoisier was arrested not for his chemistry but for his second job: he had been a member of the Ferme Generale, the private syndicate that collected taxes for the crown before the Revolution. Revolutionary courts treated tax farming as a crime against the people regardless of what else a man had done with his life.

On 8 May 1794 he and twenty seven other former tax farmers were tried and guillotined the same day, the whole proceeding finished within hours. The mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange is said to have remarked that it took only a moment to cut off Lavoisier's head, and a hundred years might not produce another like it. Lavoisier had already renamed oxygen and overturned the phlogiston theory of combustion.

Benito Mussolini was captured on 27 April 1945 near Dongo, on Lake Como, while trying to flee north disguised in a German soldier's overcoat as part of a retreating convoy. Italian partisans recognised him despite the disguise, and the following day he and his mistress, Claretta Petacci, were shot on a country road above the lake.

Their bodies, along with those of other executed Fascist officials, were driven to Milan and hung upside down from the girders of a petrol station in the Piazzale Loreto, where a crowd that had suffered under his regime gathered to see them. The display was intended partly as retribution for an earlier massacre of partisans whose bodies had been left in the same square, and photographs of the scene circulated worldwide within days.

Catherine was a German princess, born Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst, who married into the Russian throne and then took it from her own husband. Peter III was overthrown in a palace coup organised with the help of her lover Grigory Orlov in 1762 and died in custody days later, officially of a stomach complaint that few at court believed.

She died on 17 November 1796 at the age of sixty seven after a stroke, not, as the enduring rumour has it, in any accident involving a horse; that story surfaced only after her death and has no contemporary source. Over her reign Russia's territory grew substantially through wars with the Ottoman Empire and the partitions of Poland, and she corresponded with Voltaire while running an empire still built on serf labour.

Cicero was killed on 7 December 43 BCE, hunted down while fleeing after Mark Antony placed his name on the proscription lists drawn up by the Second Triumvirate. Ancient sources say he leaned his head out of the litter carrying him and offered his throat to the soldiers rather than resist further.

On Antony's specific order his hands, the hands that had written the Philippics attacking him, were cut off along with his head and nailed up on the Rostra in the Roman Forum, the platform Cicero had once used to address the Senate. Cassius Dio adds that Antony's wife Fulvia took the severed head onto her lap and pierced the tongue with a hairpin.

Elizabeth I died at Richmond Palace on 24 March 1603, unmarried and without a named successor for most of her reign, a fact that had unsettled her court for decades. She reportedly spent her final days refusing to go to bed, sitting propped on cushions on the floor, and grew too weak to speak before the end.

Her council had already been in secret contact with James VI of Scotland, and his accession as James I was proclaimed within hours of her death, ending the Tudor line and joining the English and Scottish crowns under one monarch for the first time. The Spanish Armada's defeat in 1588 had come fifteen years earlier, in the middle of her reign, not at its close.

Henry VIII died on 28 January 1547 at Whitehall Palace, aged fifty five, weighed down by illness and obesity that had made him increasingly immobile in his final years. He had broken with the Roman Catholic Church in the early 1530s after Rome refused to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, establishing himself as head of a new Church of England largely so he could marry Anne Boleyn.

Of his six wives, two were beheaded, one died after childbirth, one was divorced, one survived him, and one marriage was annulled after months. His only son, Edward VI, inherited the throne at nine and reigned for just six years, and the crown then passed through two of Henry's daughters, Mary and Elizabeth, whose reigns did far more to shape England than his own volatile decade of marriages did.

At around half past one in the afternoon on 21 October 1805, a French marksman firing down from the rigging of the ship Redoutable hit Nelson as he walked the quarterdeck of HMS Victory. The musket ball passed through his shoulder and a lung before lodging against his spine, and the surgeon who examined him recognised the wound as fatal at once.

Nelson lived roughly three more hours below deck, long enough to be told that the British fleet had broken the combined French and Spanish line and was winning decisively. He is said to have asked his flag captain, Hardy, to kiss him, and to have said he had done his duty before he died. The victory at Trafalgar ended any serious threat of a French invasion of Britain and confirmed Royal Navy dominance at sea for the following century.

James Cook died on 14 February 1779 at Kealakekua Bay in Hawaii, on his third Pacific voyage, after charting stretches of the Pacific coastline, New Zealand and eastern Australia that no European map had recorded before him.

His crew had returned to the bay to repair a damaged mast, and after Hawaiians took a ship's boat, Cook tried to hold the local chief Kalaniopu'u hostage until it was returned. A crowd on the beach turned on him; he was stabbed and clubbed in the shallows, and four marines and at least seventeen Hawaiians also died in the fighting.

Leonidas died holding the pass at Thermopylae in 480 BCE after a local shepherd, Ephialtes, showed Persian forces a mountain track that let them encircle the defenders. Herodotus records that Leonidas sent most of his allied troops away once the position was lost and stayed with a much smaller core, roughly the three hundred Spartans plus other holdouts, to fight to the end.

The Persians beheaded his body and displayed the head on a stake, an act Herodotus presents as unusual cruelty by Xerxes' own standards. Decades later the Spartans recovered his remains and reburied him at home, and the site still carries an inscribed epitaph honouring those who obeyed the order to stand and not retreat.

Nelson Mandela died at his home in Johannesburg on 5 December 2013 at the age of 95, after months of declining health that had included repeated hospital admissions for a recurring lung infection linked to tuberculosis he contracted during his 27 years in prison. His death prompted ten days of national mourning in South Africa and drew more than 90 heads of state to his memorial service.

He had stepped back from public life years earlier, making his last major appearance at the 2010 World Cup that South Africa hosted, but his death still forced the country to confront how much of its post-apartheid identity had been built around him personally. He was buried in his childhood village of Qunu in the Eastern Cape, according to his own wishes, rather than in a state monument.

Saddam Hussein was executed by hanging before dawn on 30 December 2006 at a former intelligence headquarters in Baghdad that Iraqis had once feared as a place of torture. He had been convicted weeks earlier for ordering the killing of 148 Shia villagers from Dujail in 1982, in reprisal for an assassination attempt against him there.

A mobile phone video of the execution, filmed by someone present despite an official ban on recording, showed guards taunting him in his final moments and leaked within hours, prompting an Iraqi investigation into who had filmed it. His body was returned to his home region near Tikrit and buried close to his sons, who had been killed by American forces in 2003.

Sitting Bull was killed before dawn on 15 December 1890 at his cabin on the Standing Rock Reservation. Indian agency police, sent by agent James McLaughlin, who wrongly suspected him of planning to join the Ghost Dance movement and flee the reservation, came to arrest him.

He went with the officers without resistance, but his followers gathered outside and a shot was fired in the crowd. In the fighting that followed, Sitting Bull was shot twice and killed along with thirteen others, among them his son Crow Foot. Two weeks later, soldiers killed roughly 150 to 300 Lakota men, women, and children at Wounded Knee.

Spartacus, a Thracian gladiator, led an escape from a training school at Capua in 73 BCE that grew into an army of escaped slaves numbering in the tens of thousands. Rome sent successive commanders against him before finally committing Marcus Licinius Crassus with a force large enough to end the revolt in 71 BCE.

According to the historian Appian, Spartacus was wounded in the thigh in the final battle, sank to one knee behind his shield, and was killed along with most of his remaining fighters; his body was never identified afterward. Six thousand of his surviving followers were crucified along the Appian Way, a line of crosses stretching for miles as a deliberate warning to travellers.

Suleiman died on the night of 6 to 7 September 1566 in his tent outside the fortress of Szigetvar, in his seventies and on his thirteenth military campaign, having pushed Ottoman territory to its greatest extent and overseen a major reform of the empire's legal code. His advisers, judging that news of his death would collapse morale mid-siege, kept the body inside the tent and continued issuing orders in his name.

The concealment held for weeks: meals were still delivered to the tent, and daily routines were kept up as though the sultan were merely unwell, while the army pressed the siege to its conclusion before the news finally broke. His heart and other organs, according to tradition, were buried near the site of the camp, separate from the tomb built for the rest of him in Istanbul.

Thomas More was executed on 6 July 1535 on Tower Hill, beheaded for refusing to swear the Oath of Succession recognising Henry VIII as head of the Church of England. More had been the king's Lord Chancellor and had once been a close friend, but he would not sign an oath he believed denied the authority of the Pope.

He had written Utopia in 1516, a fictional account of an island society without private property, intended partly as satire and partly as a genuine thought experiment about how a state might be organised differently. More was tried on the testimony of a single witness, Richard Rich, whose account he disputed to the end, and reportedly told the crowd at his execution that he died the king's good servant, but God's first.

William Wallace was captured near Glasgow in August 1305, betrayed by a Scottish knight loyal to England, and taken to London for trial. He was tried for treason despite never having sworn allegiance to Edward I, a distinction that made little difference to the outcome: the verdict and sentence were decided before the trial began.

On 23 August 1305 he was dragged through London tied to a horse, then hanged, drawn and quartered at Smithfield, a punishment reserved for the worst offences against the crown. His head was set on London Bridge and his limbs displayed in Newcastle, Berwick, Stirling and Perth, a deliberate warning that instead helped make him a lasting symbol of Scottish resistance.

Xerxes was murdered in his own bedchamber in 465 BCE, not on any battlefield he had commanded personally. The killer was Artabanus, the commander of his royal bodyguard, who according to ancient accounts acted with a eunuch's help and then briefly tried to seize power himself by pinning the murder on Xerxes' son Darius.

The plot unravelled within months; another son, who took the throne as Artaxerxes I, had Artabanus killed once the truth came out. It was an unglamorous end for a king remembered abroad chiefly for the failed invasion of Greece a decade and a half earlier, and Persian court sources on his final years are thin compared with the Greek accounts of Thermopylae and Salamis.
